docs.title: NetTap
docs.text:
Open-source network visibility for your home or small business.

NetTap is a hardware-agnostic network appliance for your home or office network. It captures and analyzes your network traffic, giving you enterprise-grade telemetry through a polished web dashboard --- without requiring deep networking knowledge.

A short tour of the NetTap dashboard: Home, the Live monitor globe, Devices, Alerts, Threats and Certificates.

The tour and screenshots use demo data, not a real network.

docs.title: What NetTap Does
docs.text:
NetTap gets a copy of your network traffic in one of three ways:

  • Mirror / SPAN (recommended): a managed switch copies traffic to NetTap. NetTap stays outside the traffic path, so it can't break your network. This is the tested mode.
  • DHCP gateway (being tested): NetTap hands out addresses and passes traffic on to your router. It hasn't been verified on real hardware yet.
  • Inline bridge (advanced): NetTap sits between your modem and router as a transparent Layer 2 bridge. It hasn't been verified on real hardware with the current build.

The setup guide helps you choose. Either way, NetTap inspects the traffic with industry-standard tools:

  • Zeek generates structured metadata logs for every connection (DNS, HTTP, TLS, DHCP, SMTP, and more)
  • Suricata performs signature-based intrusion detection using the Emerging Threats ruleset
  • netsniff-ng records all traffic to rotating PCAP files for forensic packet analysis
  • OpenSearch indexes everything for fast search and visualization

The result: you see exactly what every device on your network is doing, which external servers they talk to, and whether any of that traffic is suspicious.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Device-Centric Dashboard --- see what each device is doing at a glance, with bandwidth, connections, and risk scores
  • Plain English Alerts --- Suricata IDS detections with human-readable explanations, not raw signatures
  • Passive Capture --- in mirror mode NetTap only receives a copy of the traffic, so it adds no latency and can't break your network
  • Three-Tier Storage --- intelligent retention policies keep 90 days of metadata, 180 days of alerts, and 30 days of packet captures
  • SSD Health Monitoring --- SMART monitoring with automatic write coalescing to protect drive endurance
  • Built-in Update System --- check for and apply updates from the dashboard
  • No Cloud Dependency --- everything runs locally. No subscriptions, no telemetry, no data leaves your network
  • Setup Wizard --- guided first-run experience walks you through the capture mode, port choice, storage and your admin account

docs.title: Architecture at a Glance
docs.text:
Managed switch ── mirror port ──▶ [ capture port ]
(copy of the router port)                  │
                                          ▼
                                   Zeek + Suricata + netsniff-ng
                                          │
                                          ▼
                                     OpenSearch
                                          │
                                          ▼
                                   NetTap Dashboard (web UI)
                                   accessed via management NIC / Wi-Fi

This is mirror mode. In bridge mode the capture port is a bridge br0 between the modem and the router, and in DHCP gateway mode it is the one port plugged into your router. In mirror and bridge modes NetTap is invisible on the data path: your modem and router communicate exactly as before, and NetTap just listens.

docs.title: Project Status
docs.text:
NetTap is in active development. The current version is the pre-release v0.4.0-alpha.1, for early testers using mirror / SPAN mode. It covers:

  • Core infrastructure (bridge, Malcolm deployment, hardware validation)
  • Storage management (ILM policies, retention daemon, SMART monitoring)
  • Onboarding UX (setup wizard, NIC auto-detection)
  • Dashboard (live traffic, alerts, devices, investigations, compliance)
  • Community release (documentation, CI/CD, security hardening)

docs.title: Backup & Restore
docs.text:
NetTap keeps network telemetry in OpenSearch, its own settings and records in Docker volumes, and its configuration and secrets in files next to the code. This page covers how to back up and restore all three.

Every command runs on the NetTap box. Set NETTAP_DIR to wherever you cloned NetTap first. The examples use /opt/nettap; some installs use /home/nettap/NetTap:

NETTAP_DIR=/opt/nettap

docs.title: What to Back Up
docs.text:
Data Where it lives Importance Configuration and secrets $NETTAP_DIR/.env, $NETTAP_DIR/docker/.env, and the docker/auth/, docker/curlrc/, docker/certs/ and docker/ssl/ folders Critical. docker/.env is the file Docker Compose reads, and the folders hold the OpenSearch logins and TLS keys OpenSearch data docker_opensearch-data Docker volume High. All Zeek and Suricata records and the device registry NetTap records docker_nettap-appdata volume (/opt/nettap/data inside nettap-storage-daemon) Medium. Investigations, device baseline, detection packs, retention settings and excluded IPs Dashboard logins docker_web-data volume (/var/lib/nettap-web inside nettap-web) Medium. The web UI's user accounts and session key Grafana dashboards docker_grafana-data volume Low. Grafana is off by default Raw PCAP docker_pcap-data volume Usually skipped. It's large and rotates on its own

Volume names start with docker_

Docker Compose names volumes after the folder that holds docker-compose.yml, which is docker/. Check the real names with sudo docker volume ls. A command that names a volume that doesn't exist (for example opensearch-data without the prefix) silently creates a new, empty one.

Store backups somewhere other than the NetTap disk. The commands below write to /var/backups/nettap; copy that folder off the box afterwards.

docs.title: Backing Up Configuration and Secrets
docs.text:
sudo mkdir -p /var/backups/nettap
sudo tar czf /var/backups/nettap/config-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz -C "$NETTAP_DIR" \
  .env docker/.env docker/auth docker/curlrc docker/certs docker/ssl
sudo chmod 600 /var/backups/nettap/config-*.tar.gz

The archive holds passwords and private keys, so keep it private.

docs.title: Backing Up NetTap Records and Logins
docs.text:
These volumes are read through the running containers, so nothing needs to stop:

sudo sh -c 'docker exec nettap-storage-daemon tar czf - -C /opt/nettap/data . > /var/backups/nettap/appdata-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz'
sudo sh -c 'docker exec nettap-web tar czf - -C /var/lib/nettap-web . > /var/backups/nettap/webdata-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz'
sudo chmod 600 /var/backups/nettap/webdata-*.tar.gz

# Check what went in
sudo tar tzf /var/backups/nettap/appdata-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz

To restore one, copy it back in and restart the container:

sudo sh -c 'docker exec -i nettap-storage-daemon tar xzf - -C /opt/nettap/data < /var/backups/nettap/appdata-20261102.tar.gz'
sudo docker restart nettap-storage-daemon

docs.title: OpenSearch Snapshots
docs.text:
OpenSearch snapshots capture indices while NetTap keeps running. OpenSearch only answers with a login. The osapi helper below runs each call inside the OpenSearch container with the login NetTap already stores there, so you never type the password:

osapi() { sudo docker exec nettap-opensearch curl -sk --config /var/local/curlrc/.opensearch.primary.curlrc "$@"; }

A plain curl -sk https://localhost:9200/... from the host answers 401 Unauthorized.

docs.title: Setting Up a Snapshot Repository
docs.text:
Register a filesystem repository once:

osapi -X PUT "https://localhost:9200/_snapshot/nettap_backup" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"type": "fs", "settings": {"location": "/opt/opensearch/backup/nettap", "compress": true}}'

It answers {"acknowledged":true}. /opt/opensearch/backup is the docker_opensearch-backup volume, already allowed as path.repo in the compose file. On the host, the files live in /var/lib/docker/volumes/docker_opensearch-backup/_data/nettap.

docs.title: Creating a Snapshot
docs.text:
osapi -X PUT "https://localhost:9200/_snapshot/nettap_backup/snapshot_$(date +%Y%m%d)?wait_for_completion=true" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"indices": "arkime_sessions3-*,malcolm_beats_*,nettap-*", "ignore_unavailable": true, "include_global_state": false}'

The reply ends with "state":"SUCCESS" and "failed":0. Zeek logs and Suricata alerts are both in the daily arkime_sessions3-* indices; nettap-* holds the device registry and change log.

To take the snapshots off the box:

sudo tar czf /var/backups/nettap/snapshots-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz \
  -C /var/lib/docker/volumes/docker_opensearch-backup/_data nettap

docs.title: Checking Snapshots
docs.text:
# List all snapshots
osapi "https://localhost:9200/_cat/snapshots/nettap_backup?v"

# Which indices one snapshot holds
osapi "https://localhost:9200/_snapshot/nettap_backup/snapshot_20261102" | python3 -m json.tool

docs.title: Restoring from a Snapshot
docs.text:
Try a restore under a new name first. It leaves the live data alone:

osapi -X POST "https://localhost:9200/_snapshot/nettap_backup/snapshot_20261102/_restore?wait_for_completion=true" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"indices": "nettap-devices", "rename_pattern": "(.+)", "rename_replacement": "restored-$1", "include_global_state": false}'

osapi "https://localhost:9200/_cat/indices/nettap-devices,restored-nettap-devices?v&h=index,docs.count"
osapi -X DELETE "https://localhost:9200/restored-nettap-devices"

A full restore overwrites existing data

Restoring into the original names replaces what is in those indices now.

An open index can't be restored over, so close the ones you restore first:

osapi -X POST "https://localhost:9200/arkime_sessions3-*,nettap-*/_close"

osapi -X POST "https://localhost:9200/_snapshot/nettap_backup/snapshot_20261102/_restore?wait_for_completion=true" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"indices": "arkime_sessions3-*,malcolm_beats_*,nettap-*", "ignore_unavailable": true, "include_global_state": false}'

Restored indices open on their own once the restore finishes.

docs.title: Docker Volume Backup
docs.text:
A copy of the whole OpenSearch volume needs NetTap stopped. Snapshots (above) are the tested path and need no downtime.

# Stop services first
sudo systemctl stop nettap

# Back up the OpenSearch data volume
sudo docker run --rm \
  -v docker_opensearch-data:/data:ro \
  -v /var/backups/nettap:/backup \
  alpine tar czf /backup/opensearch-data-$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz -C /data .

# Restart services
sudo systemctl start nettap

docs.title: Restoring Docker Volumes
docs.text:
sudo systemctl stop nettap

sudo docker run --rm \
  -v docker_opensearch-data:/data \
  -v /var/backups/nettap:/backup \
  alpine sh -c "rm -rf /data/* && tar xzf /backup/opensearch-data-20261102.tar.gz -C /data"

sudo systemctl start nettap

After a volume restore, run the OpenSearch security bootstrap from the project README. Recreating the OpenSearch container resets its role mapping.

docs.title: Automated Backups
docs.text:
Create a cron job for daily backups:

sudo crontab -e

Add (change the path to your NETTAP_DIR):

# Daily NetTap backup at 2 AM
0 2 * * * /opt/nettap/scripts/backup.sh >> /var/log/nettap-backup.log 2>&1

Example backup script. Save it as $NETTAP_DIR/scripts/backup.sh and chmod 700 it. Cron runs it as root, so it needs no sudo:

/opt/nettap/scripts/backup.sh
#!/bin/bash
set -uo pipefail

NETTAP_DIR=/opt/nettap
BACKUP_DIR=/var/backups/nettap
DATE=$(date +%Y%m%d)
KEEP_DAYS=7

osapi() { docker exec nettap-opensearch curl -sk --config /var/local/curlrc/.opensearch.primary.curlrc "$@"; }

mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR"

# Configuration and secrets
tar czf "$BACKUP_DIR/config-$DATE.tar.gz" -C "$NETTAP_DIR" \
  .env docker/.env docker/auth docker/curlrc docker/certs docker/ssl

# NetTap records and dashboard logins
docker exec nettap-storage-daemon tar czf - -C /opt/nettap/data . > "$BACKUP_DIR/appdata-$DATE.tar.gz"
docker exec nettap-web tar czf - -C /var/lib/nettap-web . > "$BACKUP_DIR/webdata-$DATE.tar.gz"
chmod 600 "$BACKUP_DIR"/*.tar.gz

# OpenSearch snapshot (the nettap_backup repository must be registered once, see above)
osapi -X PUT "https://localhost:9200/_snapshot/nettap_backup/snapshot_$DATE?wait_for_completion=true" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"indices":"arkime_sessions3-*,malcolm_beats_*,nettap-*","ignore_unavailable":true,"include_global_state":false}' \
  | grep -q '"state":"SUCCESS"' || echo "Snapshot $DATE did not succeed"

# Drop the snapshot and archives from KEEP_DAYS ago
osapi -X DELETE "https://localhost:9200/_snapshot/nettap_backup/snapshot_$(date -d "$KEEP_DAYS days ago" +%Y%m%d)" >/dev/null
find "$BACKUP_DIR" -name "*.tar.gz" -mtime +$KEEP_DAYS -delete

echo "Backup completed: $DATE"

docs.title: Disaster Recovery
docs.text:
If the system needs a complete rebuild:

  1. Install a fresh Ubuntu Server.
  2. Clone NetTap to the same path and unpack the config archive into it: sudo tar xzf config-YYYYMMDD.tar.gz -C "$NETTAP_DIR".
  3. Run sudo scripts/install/install.sh. It keeps the restored docker/.env and secrets.
  4. Restore OpenSearch from a snapshot (register the repository, then restore) or from a volume backup.
  5. Restore the NetTap records and dashboard logins archives.
  6. Verify the data on the dashboard.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: NetTap is configured primarily through environment variables in the .env file. This page provides an overview of the configuration system.

docs.title: Configuration File
docs.text:
The main configuration file is .env in the project root (typically /opt/nettap/.env). This file is loaded by:

  • The install scripts (via scripts/common.sh)
  • Docker Compose (for container environment variables)
  • The storage daemon
# Edit configuration
sudo nano /opt/nettap/.env

# After changes, restart to apply
sudo systemctl restart nettap

Secrets in .env

The .env file contains passwords and secrets. Ensure it has restrictive permissions: 

sudo chmod 600 /opt/nettap/.env
sudo chown root:root /opt/nettap/.env

docs.title: Network Interfaces
docs.text:
.env
WAN_INTERFACE=eth0          # NIC connected to ISP modem
LAN_INTERFACE=eth1          # NIC connected to router
MGMT_INTERFACE=eth2         # Management NIC (optional)
MGMT_IP=192.168.1.100      # Static IP for management NIC
MGMT_NETMASK=255.255.255.0 # Netmask for management NIC

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
.env
NETTAP_HOSTNAME=nettap.local    # mDNS hostname
DASHBOARD_PORT=443              # HTTPS port for the dashboard

docs.title: OpenSearch
docs.text:
.env
OPENSEARCH_JAVA_OPTS="-Xms4g -Xmx4g"              # JVM heap size
OPENSEARCH_ADMIN_PASSWORD=N3tT@p_0p3n               # Admin password (auto-generated)

docs.title: Storage Retention
docs.text:
.env
RETENTION_HOT=90                    # Zeek metadata retention (days)
RETENTION_WARM=180                  # Suricata alert retention (days)
RETENTION_COLD=30                   # PCAP retention (days)
DISK_THRESHOLD_PERCENT=80           # Start pruning at this disk usage %
EMERGENCY_THRESHOLD_PERCENT=90      # Aggressive pruning threshold

docs.title: Alerting
docs.text:
.env
SMTP_HOST=                  # SMTP server for email notifications
SMTP_PORT=587               # SMTP port
SMTP_USER=                  # SMTP username
SMTP_PASS=                  # SMTP password
ALERT_EMAIL=                # Notification recipient email
WEBHOOK_URL=                # Webhook URL for alert notifications

docs.title: Container Images
docs.text:
.env
MALCOLM_IMAGE_REGISTRY=ghcr.io/idaholab/malcolm    # Malcolm container registry
MALCOLM_IMAGE_TAG=26.02.0                           # Malcolm version tag

docs.title: Daemon
docs.text:
.env
API_PORT=8880                       # Daemon API port
STORAGE_CHECK_INTERVAL=300          # Storage check frequency (seconds)
SMART_CHECK_INTERVAL=3600           # SMART check frequency (seconds)
SMART_DEVICE=/dev/nvme0n1           # Storage device to monitor
LOG_LEVEL=INFO                      # Daemon log level (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR)

For the complete reference of all environment variables, see Environment Reference.

docs.title: Applying Configuration Changes
docs.text:
Most configuration changes require a service restart:

sudo systemctl restart nettap

Some changes may require reapplying specific configurations:

Change Action Required Interface names Restart + re-run bridge setup Retention periods Restart + reapply ILM policies OpenSearch heap Restart (containers recreated) Dashboard hostname Restart + Avahi restart SMTP / webhook settings Restart daemon only Log level Restart daemon only

docs.title: Firewall Configuration
docs.text:
If UFW is active, the installer adds rules automatically. To manage manually:

# View current rules
sudo ufw status verbose

# Add dashboard access
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp comment "NetTap dashboard"

# Add Malcolm dashboards
sudo ufw allow 9443/tcp comment "Malcolm dashboards"

# Add mDNS
sudo ufw allow 5353/udp comment "mDNS (avahi)"

# Restrict dashboard to specific subnet
sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 443 proto tcp comment "NetTap dashboard (LAN only)"

The dedicated firewall setup script provides additional hardening:

sudo scripts/install/setup-firewall.sh

docs.title: Docker Compose Overrides
docs.text:
For advanced configuration, you can create a docker-compose.override.yml file alongside the main compose file:

docker/docker-compose.override.yml
services:
  opensearch:
    environment:
      OPENSEARCH_JAVA_OPTS: "-Xms8g -Xmx8g"  # Override heap size

  zeek-live:
    environment:
      ZEEK_LOCAL_NETS: "10.0.0.0/8"  # Override local network definition

Docker Compose automatically merges override files with the main configuration.

docs.title: Settings via Dashboard
docs.text:
Some settings can also be changed through the web dashboard:

  • Settings (/settings) --- general configuration
  • Notifications (/settings/notifications) --- email, webhook, and in-app notification setup
  • System (/system) --- view system health and storage status

Dashboard settings changes are persisted and take effect immediately without requiring a service restart.

docs.title: Performance Tuning
docs.text: NetTap is pre-configured for the reference Intel N100 hardware (4 cores, 16 GB RAM, 1 TB NVMe). This page covers tuning options for different hardware or workloads.

docs.title: OpenSearch JVM Heap
docs.text:
OpenSearch is the largest memory consumer. The JVM heap size controls how much RAM OpenSearch uses for indexing and search operations.

Default: 4 GB (suitable for 16 GB RAM systems)

.env
OPENSEARCH_JAVA_OPTS="-Xms4g -Xmx4g"

docs.title: Sizing Guidelines
docs.text:
System RAM Recommended Heap Notes 8 GB 2--3 GB Tight --- may struggle under heavy load 16 GB 4 GB Default. Good balance for most home networks 32 GB 8 GB Faster queries, larger working set in memory 64 GB+ 16 GB max OpenSearch does not benefit from heaps > 32 GB

Heap must not exceed 50% of system RAM

Other services (Zeek, Suricata, the OS) also need memory. As a rule, set OpenSearch heap to no more than 50% of total RAM, and never more than 32 GB.

After changing, restart services:

sudo systemctl restart nettap

docs.title: Logstash JVM Heap
docs.text:
Logstash processes and enriches logs before they reach OpenSearch.

Default: 2 GB

.env
LS_JAVA_OPTS="-Xmx2g -Xms2g"
System RAM Recommended 8 GB 1 GB 16 GB 2 GB 32 GB 2--4 GB

docs.title: Kernel Parameters
docs.text:
The installer applies these kernel tuning parameters in /etc/sysctl.d/99-nettap.conf:

/etc/sysctl.d/99-nettap.conf
# Required by OpenSearch
vm.max_map_count = 262144

# Increase network buffer sizes for high-throughput capture
net.core.rmem_max = 134217728
net.core.wmem_max = 134217728
net.core.rmem_default = 16777216
net.core.netdev_max_backlog = 5000

# Increase conntrack table for busy networks
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 1048576

docs.title: Bridge-Specific Tuning
docs.text:
The bridge setup script applies these in /etc/sysctl.d/99-nettap-bridge.conf:

/etc/sysctl.d/99-nettap-bridge.conf
# Disable bridge netfilter — avoid iptables overhead on bridged traffic
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 0
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables = 0
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-arptables = 0

# Disable IPv6 on bridge to stay invisible
net.ipv6.conf.br0.disable_ipv6 = 1

To verify current values:

sysctl vm.max_map_count
sysctl net.core.rmem_max
sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables

docs.title: NIC Offload Settings
docs.text:
The bridge setup script disables hardware offloads that interfere with accurate packet capture:

# Applied automatically during bridge setup
ethtool -K eth0 tso off gso off gro off lro off
ethtool -K eth1 tso off gso off gro off lro off

# Increase RX ring buffer for better capture under burst
ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096
ethtool -G eth1 rx 4096

These settings reduce CPU-assisted packet assembly, ensuring Zeek and Suricata see packets as they appear on the wire.

docs.title: Verifying Offload Settings
docs.text:
ethtool -k eth0 | grep -E "tcp-segmentation|generic-segmentation|generic-receive|large-receive"
ethtool -g eth0

docs.title: Zeek Threads
docs.text:
Zeek's thread count affects how many packets it can process simultaneously. For the default configuration:

docker-compose.yml (zeek-live environment)
ZEEK_LIVE_CAPTURE: "true"
PCAP_IFACE: "br0"

On a 4-core system, Zeek typically uses 1--2 cores for capture and analysis. For higher-throughput networks, you can enable Zeek's cluster mode with worker processes.

docs.title: Suricata Threads
docs.text:
Suricata's runmode and thread settings control parallelism:

docker-compose.yml (suricata-live environment)
SURICATA_RUNMODE: "workers"   # Each thread handles capture + detection

The workers runmode is the most efficient for multi-core systems. Each worker handles its own traffic via kernel-level flow balancing (AF_PACKET cluster).

docs.title: Arkime
docs.text: Arkime is off by default (compose profile arkime), so no packet-thread tuning applies to a standard install.

docs.title: SSD Write Endurance
docs.text: NetTap includes several measures to protect SSD lifespan:

docs.title: Write Coalescing
docs.text:
• Zeek log rotation: Logs are flushed every 30 seconds (not per-event). Configured in config/zeek/nettap.zeek: 

    redef Log::default_rotation_interval = 30sec;

  • Docker log rotation: Container logs are capped at 10 MB with 3 rotations: /etc/docker/daemon.json

    {
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "10m",
    "max-file": "3"
  }
}

docs.title: SMART Monitoring
docs.text:
The daemon checks SMART health every hour (configurable):

.env
SMART_CHECK_INTERVAL=3600       # Seconds between SMART checks
SMART_DEVICE=/dev/nvme0n1       # Device to monitor

View current SMART status:

curl http://localhost:8880/api/smart/health

Or from the command line:

sudo smartctl -a /dev/nvme0n1

docs.title: PCAP Capture Settings
docs.text:
Control how raw packet capture operates:

.env
PCAP_ROTATE_MB=256      # Rotate PCAP files at this size (MB)
PCAP_ROTATE_MIN=10      # Rotate PCAP files at this interval (minutes)

Larger rotation sizes reduce file overhead but increase recovery time if a write is interrupted.

PCAP Search and TShark read a whole file at a time, and tshark needs about 120 MiB plus roughly the file's own size in memory. The TShark container has 1 GiB, so files over about 700 MB can't be searched: the search reports them as out of memory. The installer's 256 MB keeps every file searchable (about 11 s each at the container's 1 CPU).

docs.title: Hardware Watchdog
docs.text:
NetTap configures a hardware watchdog timer as a last-resort failsafe. If the system hangs, the watchdog triggers a hard reboot to restore network traffic flow.

Configuration is in config/watchdog/watchdog.conf:

Setting Default Description interval 10s How often the daemon "pets" the watchdog watchdog-timeout 60s Time without a pet before hardware reboot max-load-1 24 Reboot if 1-minute load average exceeds this ping 127.0.0.1 Test kernel network stack is alive

The watchdog runs with realtime scheduling priority to ensure it functions even under extreme system load.

docs.title: Resource Monitoring
docs.text:
Check system resource usage:

# Overall system status
htop

# Docker container resource usage
docker stats --no-stream

# OpenSearch cluster health
curl -sk https://localhost:9200/_cluster/health | python3 -m json.tool

# OpenSearch node stats
curl -sk https://localhost:9200/_nodes/stats/jvm | python3 -m json.tool

docs.title: TLS Certificates
docs.text: NetTap uses HTTPS for all dashboard and API access. By default, a self-signed certificate is generated during installation. This page covers how to configure custom certificates.

docs.title: Default Setup
docs.text:
During installation, scripts/generate-cert.sh creates a self-signed TLS certificate and key:

  • Certificate: docker/ssl/nettap.crt
  • Private key: docker/ssl/nettap.key

The nginx reverse proxy (nettap-nginx) uses these files for TLS termination on port 443.

Browser warnings

Self-signed certificates cause browser security warnings. This is expected and safe for LAN-only access. You can add a permanent exception in your browser, or replace the certificate with one trusted by your devices.

docs.title: Option 1: Let's Encrypt (via DNS challenge)
docs.text:
If you have a domain name and can configure DNS, you can use Let's Encrypt for a free, trusted certificate. Since NetTap is typically not publicly accessible, use a DNS-01 challenge:

# Install certbot with DNS plugin (example: Cloudflare)
sudo apt install certbot python3-certbot-dns-cloudflare

# Create credentials file
cat > /etc/letsencrypt/cloudflare.ini << EOF
dns_cloudflare_api_token = your-cloudflare-api-token
EOF
chmod 600 /etc/letsencrypt/cloudflare.ini

# Request certificate
sudo certbot certonly \
  --dns-cloudflare \
  --dns-cloudflare-credentials /etc/letsencrypt/cloudflare.ini \
  -d nettap.yourdomain.com

# Copy to NetTap SSL directory
sudo cp /etc/letsencrypt/live/nettap.yourdomain.com/fullchain.pem /opt/nettap/docker/ssl/nettap.crt
sudo cp /etc/letsencrypt/live/nettap.yourdomain.com/privkey.pem /opt/nettap/docker/ssl/nettap.key

# Restart nginx
docker restart nettap-nginx

docs.title: Option 2: Private CA
docs.text:
If you run a private certificate authority (e.g., with step-ca, mkcert, or Active Directory Certificate Services):

# Generate a certificate signed by your CA
# ... (depends on your CA tool)

# Copy certificate and key
sudo cp your-cert.pem /opt/nettap/docker/ssl/nettap.crt
sudo cp your-key.pem /opt/nettap/docker/ssl/nettap.key

# Set permissions
sudo chmod 644 /opt/nettap/docker/ssl/nettap.crt
sudo chmod 600 /opt/nettap/docker/ssl/nettap.key

# Restart nginx
docker restart nettap-nginx

docs.title: Option 3: mkcert (Development/Home Use)
docs.text:
mkcert creates locally-trusted certificates. Install the root CA on your devices once, then all certificates it issues are trusted:

# Install mkcert
sudo apt install libnss3-tools
wget https://github.com/FiloSottile/mkcert/releases/latest/download/mkcert-linux-amd64
chmod +x mkcert-linux-amd64
sudo mv mkcert-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/mkcert

# Install the root CA (do this on the NetTap host)
mkcert -install

# Generate certificate
mkcert -cert-file /opt/nettap/docker/ssl/nettap.crt \
       -key-file /opt/nettap/docker/ssl/nettap.key \
       nettap.local 192.168.1.100 localhost

# Restart nginx
docker restart nettap-nginx

Then install the mkcert root CA (~/.local/share/mkcert/rootCA.pem) on each device that accesses the dashboard.

docs.title: Certificate Requirements
docs.text:
The certificate must:

  • Be in PEM format
  • Include the hostname or IP used to access the dashboard in the Subject Alternative Name (SAN)
  • Have the private key unencrypted (no passphrase)

Common SANs to include:

  • nettap.local (mDNS hostname)
  • The management IP address (e.g., 192.168.1.100)
  • localhost (for local access)

docs.title: Regenerating the Self-Signed Certificate
docs.text:
To regenerate the default self-signed certificate:

sudo scripts/generate-cert.sh
docker restart nettap-nginx

docs.title: Malcolm TLS
docs.text:
The Malcolm stack (accessible on port 9443) uses its own TLS certificates generated during Malcolm deployment. These are stored in the MALCOLM_CERTS_DIR (default: docker/certs/) and are separate from the NetTap dashboard certificate.

To access Malcolm dashboards without certificate warnings, you would need to replace the Malcolm certificates as well. Refer to the Malcolm documentation for details.

docs.title: Verifying Certificates
docs.text:
# Check the current certificate
openssl x509 -in /opt/nettap/docker/ssl/nettap.crt -text -noout

# Test the HTTPS connection
curl -vk https://localhost:443 2>&1 | grep -E "subject|issuer|expire"

# Check certificate expiry
openssl x509 -in /opt/nettap/docker/ssl/nettap.crt -enddate -noout

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common issues and their solutions.

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• Browser shows "connection refused" or timeout
  • https://nettap.local does not resolve

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
# Check if the service is running
systemctl status nettap

# Check if containers are running
docker compose -f /opt/nettap/docker/docker-compose.yml ps

# Check the nginx proxy specifically
docker logs nettap-nginx --tail 20

# Check if port 443 is listening
ss -tlnp | grep 443

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text: Cause Solution Service not started sudo systemctl start nettap Nginx container not running docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d nettap-nginx Port conflict on 443 Check for other services using port 443: ss -tlnp \| grep 443 mDNS not working Try the IP address directly: https://192.168.1.100 Avahi not running sudo systemctl restart avahi-daemon

docs.title: "OpenSearch not responding"
docs.text:
OpenSearch takes 2--5 minutes to start, especially on first boot when it initializes security indices.

# Check OpenSearch health
curl -sk https://localhost:9200/_cluster/health | python3 -m json.tool

# Check OpenSearch logs
docker logs nettap-opensearch --tail 50

# Check JVM memory
docker stats nettap-opensearch --no-stream

docs.title: "Cluster health: yellow"
docs.text: Yellow cluster health is normal and expected for a single-node deployment. It means all primary shards are assigned, but replicas cannot be allocated (because there is only one node). This does not affect functionality.

docs.title: OpenSearch Out of Memory (OOM)
docs.text:
If OpenSearch is killed by the OOM killer:

# Check if OOM occurred
dmesg | grep -i "oom\|killed"
journalctl -k | grep -i "oom\|killed"

Solution: Reduce the JVM heap size or add more RAM:

.env
# Reduce to 3 GB on a 16 GB system
OPENSEARCH_JAVA_OPTS="-Xms3g -Xmx3g"

Then restart: sudo systemctl restart nettap

docs.title: vm.max_map_count Error
docs.text:
OpenSearch requires vm.max_map_count >= 262144. If you see:

max virtual memory areas vm.max_map_count [65530] is too low

Solution:

sudo sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=262144
echo "vm.max_map_count = 262144" | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-nettap.conf

docs.title: Traffic Not Passing Through
docs.text:
# Validate the bridge
sudo scripts/bridge/setup-bridge.sh --validate-only

# Check bridge status
ip link show br0
bridge link show

# Check that interfaces are attached
ip link show eth0 | grep master
ip link show eth1 | grep master

docs.title: Bridge Validation Failures
docs.text: Issue Cause Solution Bridge not found Bridge was not created Re-run: sudo scripts/bridge/setup-bridge.sh --wan eth0 --lan eth1 Interface not attached NIC removed from bridge Re-run bridge setup STP enabled STP should be off for inline tap ip link set br0 type bridge stp_state 0 Forward delay non-zero Should be 0 for inline tap ip link set br0 type bridge forward_delay 0 Promiscuous mode off Required for packet capture ip link set eth0 promisc on; ip link set eth1 promisc on

docs.title: Bridge Lost After Reboot
docs.text:
If the bridge does not persist across reboots, the netplan configuration may be missing:

# Check for netplan config
cat /etc/netplan/10-nettap-bridge.yaml

# If missing, re-run with persistence
sudo scripts/bridge/setup-bridge.sh --wan eth0 --lan eth1 --persist

docs.title: Tearing Down the Bridge
docs.text:
If you need to remove the bridge and restore normal networking:

sudo scripts/bridge/setup-bridge.sh --teardown

This removes the bridge, restores interfaces, and cleans up persistence files.

docs.title: Containers Failing to Start
docs.text:
# Check which containers are unhealthy or restarting
docker compose -f /opt/nettap/docker/docker-compose.yml ps

# Check logs for a specific container
docker logs nettap-opensearch --tail 50
docker logs nettap-zeek-live --tail 50
docker logs nettap-suricata-live --tail 50

docs.title: Zeek or Suricata Not Capturing
docs.text:
# Check if br0 exists and is up
ip link show br0

# Check if capture containers can see the interface
docker exec nettap-zeek-live ip link show

# Check Zeek logs
docker logs nettap-zeek-live --tail 30

# Check Suricata stats
docker logs nettap-suricata-live --tail 30

Tip

Zeek and Suricata run with network_mode: host so they can access the bridge interface directly. If the bridge is not set up, they will fail to start capture.

docs.title: Restarting Individual Containers
docs.text:
# Restart a specific container
docker compose -f /opt/nettap/docker/docker-compose.yml restart zeek-live

# Restart the whole stack
sudo systemctl restart nettap

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• Dashboard shows "--" for all values
  • "No traffic data available" messages

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
1. Check that containers are running: 

    docker compose -f /opt/nettap/docker/docker-compose.yml ps

  2. Check that OpenSearch has indices: 

    curl -sk https://localhost:9200/_cat/indices?v

  3. Check that the daemon API is reachable: 

    curl http://localhost:8880/api/health

  4. Check Zeek log output: 

    docker exec nettap-zeek-live ls -la /zeek/live/

docs.title: Common Causes
docs.text: Cause Solution Bridge not set up Run bridge setup script No traffic on bridge Verify cables are connected to WAN and LAN ports OpenSearch still starting Wait 5 minutes for initial startup Filebeat not shipping logs Check docker logs nettap-filebeat Logstash pipeline error Check docker logs nettap-logstash Daemon not running Check docker logs nettap-storage-daemon

docs.title: "Unable to reach the monitoring daemon"
docs.text:
This warning banner appears on the dashboard when the web UI cannot reach the storage daemon API.

# Check daemon container
docker logs nettap-storage-daemon --tail 30

# Test API directly
curl http://localhost:8880/api/health

docs.title: API Returns Errors
docs.text:
# Check daemon health
curl http://localhost:8880/api/system/health | python3 -m json.tool

docs.title: High CPU Usage
docs.text:
# Check which containers use the most CPU
docker stats --no-stream --format "table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}"

Common CPU hogs:

  • Suricata under heavy traffic --- normal, scales with traffic volume
  • OpenSearch during indexing --- normal, especially after startup
  • Logstash during log enrichment --- reduce pipeline.workers if needed

docs.title: High Memory Usage
docs.text:
# Check memory per container
docker stats --no-stream --format "table {{.Name}}\t{{.MemUsage}}\t{{.MemPerc}}"

If memory is tight, reduce OpenSearch and Logstash heap sizes. See Performance Tuning.

docs.title: Disk Space Running Low
docs.text:
# Check disk usage
df -h /

# Check Docker disk usage
docker system df

# Clean up unused Docker resources
docker system prune --volumes

Warning

docker system prune --volumes removes all unused volumes, including any data not associated with a running container. Make sure all your containers are running before pruning.

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
If these troubleshooting steps do not resolve your issue:

  1. Collect diagnostic information: 

    systemctl status nettap
docker compose -f /opt/nettap/docker/docker-compose.yml ps
curl http://localhost:8880/api/system/health 2>/dev/null || echo "Daemon unreachable"
sudo scripts/bridge/setup-bridge.sh --validate-only 2>/dev/null || echo "Bridge issues"

  2. Open a GitHub Issue with the diagnostic output.

  3. Join the Discord community for real-time help.

docs.title: Updating NetTap
docs.text: NetTap includes a built-in software update system that tracks component versions, checks for updates, and applies them from the dashboard.

docs.title: Update System Overview
docs.text:
The update system manages three categories of components:

Category Components Core NetTap daemon, web dashboard Docker Images Malcolm containers (Zeek, Suricata, OpenSearch, etc.), Grafana System Docker Engine, Docker Compose, OS packages

docs.title: Via Dashboard
docs.text:
1. Navigate to System > Software Updates (/system/updates)
  2. The version inventory shows all tracked components with their current versions and status
  3. Click Check for Updates to scan for available updates

Components are grouped by category (Core, Docker Images, System) for easy review.

docs.title: Via API
docs.text:
# Get current component versions
curl http://localhost:8880/api/updates/versions

# Check for available updates
curl -X POST http://localhost:8880/api/updates/check

# Get available updates
curl http://localhost:8880/api/updates/available

docs.title: Via Command Line
docs.text:
# Pull latest repository changes
cd /opt/nettap
git pull origin main

# Pull updated Docker images
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml pull

# Restart services
sudo systemctl restart nettap

docs.title: Via Dashboard
docs.text:
1. After checking for updates, available updates appear in the update panel
  2. Select which components to update (or select all)
  3. Click Apply Updates
  4. The system creates a backup, pulls new images, and restarts affected containers
  5. Progress and status are shown in real-time

docs.title: Via Command Line
docs.text:
cd /opt/nettap

# Pull latest code
git pull origin main

# Pull updated container images
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml pull

# Restart with new images
sudo systemctl restart nettap

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: If an update causes issues, you can roll back individual components:

docs.title: Via Dashboard
docs.text: On the Software Updates page, each component shows a Rollback option if a previous version is available. Click it to revert to the prior version.

docs.title: Via Command Line
docs.text:
# Roll back to a specific Malcolm version
# Edit docker-compose.yml and change the tag
# x-malcolm-tag: &malcolm-tag "26.01.0"  # previous version

# Then restart
sudo systemctl restart nettap

docs.title: Update Schedule
docs.text:
NetTap does not auto-update. You control when updates are applied. We recommend:

  • Check weekly for security updates
  • Review release notes before applying updates
  • Back up before major version upgrades (see Backup & Restore)
  • Test in off-hours when brief service interruptions are acceptable

docs.title: Malcolm Version Pinning
docs.text:
NetTap pins Malcolm container images to a specific tested release tag (currently 26.02.0). This prevents upstream breaking changes from affecting your installation.

The tag is configured in docker/docker-compose.yml:

x-malcolm-tag: &malcolm-tag "26.02.0"

When a new Malcolm release is tested and validated with NetTap, the pinned version is updated in the repository.

Do not change the Malcolm tag manually

Changing the Malcolm image tag to an untested version may cause compatibility issues with NetTap's configuration and dashboard integrations.

docs.title: Update History
docs.text:
The Software Updates page maintains a history of applied updates, showing:

  • Component name
  • Previous version
  • New version
  • Timestamp
  • Success or failure status

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page provides a deep-dive into the NetTap system architecture, covering the network layer, data pipeline, storage tiers, and service topology.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
                        │              NetTap Appliance               │
ISP Modem ──────────────┤                                             │
          eth0 (WAN)    │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐  │
                        │  │         br0 (Transparent Bridge)      │  │
          eth1 (LAN)    │  │   STP off | FwdDelay 0 | Promisc on  │  │
Router ─────────────────┤  └──────────────┬───────────────────────┘  │
                        │                 │ Promiscuous capture       │
                        │    ┌────────────┼────────────┐             │
                        │    │            │            │             │
                        │    ▼            ▼            ▼             │
                        │  Zeek       Suricata      netsniff-ng      │
                        │  (metadata)  (IDS)       (PCAP)           │
                        │    │            │            │             │
                        │    ▼            ▼            ▼             │
                        │  Filebeat ─── Logstash ──► OpenSearch     │
                        │                               │            │
                        │              ┌────────────────┤            │
                        │              ▼                ▼            │
                        │         NetTap Web       Grafana           │
                        │         Dashboard        Dashboards        │
                        │              │                             │
          eth2 (MGMT)   │              │                             │
Dashboard Access ───────┤    nettap-nginx (TLS termination)         │
                        └───────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Transparent Bridge
docs.text:
NetTap creates a Linux software bridge (br0) binding two physical NICs. This bridge operates at Layer 2, transparently forwarding all Ethernet frames between the WAN and LAN interfaces.

Key properties:

  • No IP address on bridge --- the appliance is invisible on the data path
  • STP disabled --- no learning delay; immediate forwarding
  • Forward delay = 0 --- packets are forwarded without any hold-time
  • Multicast snooping disabled --- all multicast passes through transparently
  • MAC ageing disabled --- no MAC table expiry (reduces jitter)
  • Promiscuous mode --- both NICs capture all frames, not just those addressed to them
  • IPv6 disabled on br0 --- prevents the bridge from being discoverable

docs.title: Performance Tuning
docs.text:
The bridge setup script applies NIC-level tuning:

  • Hardware offloads disabled (TSO, GSO, GRO, LRO) --- ensures Zeek and Suricata see actual wire-format packets
  • RX ring buffer increased to 4096 entries --- prevents packet drops during traffic bursts
  • Bridge netfilter disabled --- bypasses iptables processing for bridged traffic (significant performance improvement)

docs.title: Management Interface
docs.text: A separate network interface (3rd NIC, Wi-Fi, or VLAN) provides dashboard access. This interface has an IP address and is not part of the bridge.

docs.title: Data Pipeline
docs.text: The data flows through these stages:

docs.title: 1. Packet Capture
docs.text:
Three capture engines run simultaneously with network_mode: host to directly access the bridge interface:

Engine Container Purpose Zeek nettap-zeek-live Generates structured metadata logs for every connection Suricata nettap-suricata-live IDS alerting using Emerging Threats ruleset netsniff-ng nettap-pcap-capture Raw PCAP file capture

docs.title: 2. Log Collection
docs.text:
Filebeat (nettap-filebeat) monitors the Zeek and Suricata log directories via shared Docker volumes:

  • zeek-live-logs --- Zeek JSON log files
  • suricata-live-logs --- Suricata Eve JSON files

Filebeat ships log events to Logstash for enrichment.

docs.title: 3. Log Enrichment
docs.text:
Logstash (nettap-logstash) processes and enriches logs:

  • GeoIP lookups (country, city, ASN)
  • OUI lookups (MAC address to manufacturer)
  • Severity scoring
  • Field normalization

Enriched events are indexed into OpenSearch.

docs.title: 4. Storage and Indexing
docs.text:
OpenSearch (nettap-opensearch) stores all indexed data:

  • arkime_sessions3-YYMMDD --- one daily index holding every Zeek log and Suricata alert (Malcolm's name; hot tier, deleted after RETENTION_HOT days)
  • malcolm_beats_* --- host data, when present (hot tier)
  • nettap-devices, nettap-changelog-* --- NetTap's device registry and change log

PCAP is not indexed: netsniff-ng writes files under /opt/nettap/pcap.

docs.title: 5. Visualization
docs.text:
Two visualization layers:

  • NetTap Dashboard (nettap-web) --- SvelteKit-based custom dashboard querying OpenSearch via the daemon API
  • Grafana (nettap-grafana) --- Enhanced dashboards for network overview, bandwidth trending, GeoIP maps, security alerts, and system health

docs.text:

Capture containers (Zeek, Suricata, pcap-capture) have no service dependencies --- they start immediately and write to shared volumes.

docs.title: Three-Tier Model
docs.text: Tier Where Data Type Retention Hot arkime_sessions3-* (one daily index) Zeek logs and Suricata alerts 90 days (RETENTION_HOT) Warm suricata-* Separate Suricata indices; a Malcolm install creates none 180 days (RETENTION_WARM) Cold /opt/nettap/pcap files Raw PCAP of all traffic 30 days (RETENTION_COLD) and PCAP_MAX_DISK_PCT

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Each tier has an OpenSearch ISM (Index State Management) policy defined in config/opensearch/ilm-policy.json:

  • Hot policy: Rollover at 10 GB or 1 day, delete after 90 days
  • Warm policy: Rollover at 5 GB or 1 day, force-merge and read-only after 7 days, delete after 180 days
  • Cold policy: Rollover at 20 GB or 1 day, delete after 30 days

docs.title: Disk Safety
docs.text:
The storage daemon (nettap-storage-daemon) runs a maintenance cycle every 5 minutes:

  1. Check disk utilization against threshold (80% warning, 90% emergency)
  2. If above threshold, identify and delete oldest expired indices
  3. Report status via the /api/storage/status endpoint

docs.title: Container Hardening
docs.text:
All containers follow these security practices:

  • no-new-privileges: true --- prevents privilege escalation
  • cap_drop: ALL --- drops all Linux capabilities by default
  • Capabilities added back only where required (e.g., NET_RAW for capture)
  • read_only: true with explicit tmpfs mounts where write access is needed
  • Internal services are not exposed to the host network

docs.title: Network Isolation
docs.text:
• OpenSearch port 9200 is bound to 127.0.0.1 only --- never exposed externally
  • The daemon API (port 8880) is only exposed to other containers, not ports mapped to the host
  • Dashboard access is via the nginx reverse proxy with TLS termination

docs.title: Bridge Security
docs.text:
The bridge itself is hardened:

  • No IP addresses on the bridge interface (invisible on the network)
  • IPv6 disabled on the bridge
  • Bridge netfilter disabled (no iptables interference)

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Thank you for your interest in contributing to NetTap. This page provides a summary of the contribution workflow. For full details, see the CONTRIBUTING.md file in the repository.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository on GitHub
  2. Clone your fork: 
    git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/NetTap.git
cd NetTap
  3. Add upstream remote: 
    git remote add upstream https://github.com/EliasMarine/NetTap.git
  4. Create a feature branch from develop: 
    git checkout develop
git pull upstream develop
git checkout -b phase-N/your-feature
  5. Make your changes, commit, and push
  6. Open a Pull Request targeting develop

docs.title: Branch Model
docs.text: Branch Purpose main Protected. Only receives merges at major releases. Never push directly. develop Integration branch. All feature branches merge here via PR. phase-N/description Feature branches. All work happens here. infra/description Cross-cutting infrastructure work. chore/description Maintenance tasks.

docs.title: Commit Convention
docs.text:
This project uses Conventional Commits. Every commit must follow this format:

type(scope): short description

Types: feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore, ci, perf, style

Examples:

feat(bridge): add netplan persistence for br0
fix(daemon): handle OpenSearch connection timeout
test(storage): add coverage for disk threshold logic
docs(readme): update architecture diagram
chore(docker): pin Malcolm images to v26.02.0

Rules:

  • Use imperative mood ("add" not "added")
  • No period at the end of the subject line
  • Keep subject under 72 characters
  • One logical change per commit

docs.title: Pull Request Process
docs.text:
1. Target develop --- never main
  2. Ensure your branch is up to date with develop
  3. All CI checks must pass before review
  4. Fill out the PR template completely
  5. Request a review from @EliasMarine
  6. Address review feedback with new commits (do not force-push during review)
  7. After merge, delete your feature branch

docs.title: PR Size
docs.text:
• Keep PRs under ~400 lines of diff when possible
  • Break large changes into smaller, reviewable PRs
  • Each PR should represent one logical unit of work

docs.title: Python (daemon)
docs.text:
• Linter/formatter: Ruff
  • Follow PEP 8
  • Type hints for function signatures
  • Google-style docstrings
# Same ruff version CI pins; formatter output differs between releases
uvx ruff@0.17.3 check daemon/
uvx ruff@0.17.3 format daemon/

docs.text:
• Linter: ESLint
  • Type checking: svelte-check

cd web
npm run lint
npm run check

docs.title: Shell Scripts
docs.text:
• Linter: ShellCheck
  • Use set -euo pipefail
  • Quote all variables
  • Use #!/usr/bin/env bash
shellcheck scripts/**/*.sh

docs.title: Testing Requirements
docs.text:
• All existing tests must pass before submitting a PR
  • New features must include tests
  • Bug fixes should include a regression test

See Testing for details on running the test suite.

  • Features: Open a Discussion or Issue describing the use case
  • Security: See SECURITY.md for responsible disclosure

docs.title: Settings
Release Process
docs.text: This page documents how NetTap releases are versioned, built, and published.

docs.title: Versioning Scheme
docs.text:
NetTap uses phase-based semantic versioning. Development versions increment with each phase milestone:

Milestone Version Tag Location Phase 1 complete (Core Infrastructure) v0.1.0 main Phase 2 complete (Storage Management) v0.2.0 main Phase 3 complete (Onboarding UX) v0.3.0 main Phase 4 complete (Dashboard Polish) v0.4.0 main Phase 5 complete (Community Release) v1.0.0 main

docs.title: Patch Versions
docs.text: Hotfixes within a phase use patch versions: v0.1.1, v0.1.2, etc.

docs.title: Pre-Release Versions
docs.text:
Testing releases use pre-release suffixes:

  • v1.0.0-alpha.1 --- early testing, features incomplete
  • v1.0.0-beta.1 --- feature complete, bug fixing
  • v1.0.0-rc.1 --- release candidate, final testing

docs.title: Branch Strategy
docs.text:
main ──●────●────●────●──── tag v0.4.0 ────●────●──── tag v1.0.0
        \  /      \  /                      \  /
   feature/a    fix/b                    feature/c
  • NetTap is trunk-based: main is the only long-lived branch (no develop since 2026-10-27)
  • All development happens on short-lived feature/, fix/, chore/, docs/ branches that squash-merge into main via PR
  • Phase tags are applied on main when all tasks for that phase are merged
  • Full rules: .claude/rules/git-workflow.md

docs.title: Tagging a Phase Milestone
docs.text:
When all tasks for a phase are complete and merged to main:

git checkout main
git pull origin main

# Create annotated tag
git tag -a v0.X.0 -m "Phase X: Description of milestone"

# Push the tag
git push origin v0.X.0

docs.title: Creating a GitHub Release
docs.text:
1. Go to Releases on GitHub
  2. Click "Draft a new release"
  3. Select the tag (e.g., v0.3.0)
  4. Write release notes summarizing:
  5. New features
  6. Bug fixes
  7. Breaking changes (if any)
  8. Upgrade instructions
  9. Publish the release

docs.title: Docker Image Publishing
docs.text:
Docker images are built and tagged for each release:

# Build images
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml build

# Tag with version
docker tag nettap/storage-daemon:latest nettap/storage-daemon:v0.3.0
docker tag nettap/web:latest nettap/web:v0.3.0

# Push to registry (if applicable)
docker push nettap/storage-daemon:v0.3.0
docker push nettap/web:v0.3.0

docs.title: Changelog Generation
docs.text:
NetTap uses git-cliff to generate changelogs from conventional commit messages:

# Generate changelog for all versions
git cliff -o CHANGELOG.md

# Generate changelog for a specific version range
git cliff v0.2.0..v0.3.0

# Preview changelog without writing
git cliff --unreleased

The conventional commit types map to changelog sections:

Commit Type Changelog Section feat Features fix Bug Fixes perf Performance docs Documentation refactor Refactoring test Testing chore, ci Miscellaneous

docs.title: CI/CD Pipeline
docs.text: GitHub Actions automates the build and test pipeline:

docs.title: On Every Push / PR

1. Lint: ShellCheck, Ruff, ESLint
  2. Test: pytest, Vitest, svelte-check
  3. Build: Docker images compile successfully

docs.title: On Tag Push

1. All of the above
  2. Docker build and push to container registry
  3. GitHub Release draft creation

docs.title: Malcolm Stack
docs.text:
Malcolm container images are pinned to a tested release tag in docker-compose.yml:

x-malcolm-tag: &malcolm-tag "26.02.0"

This prevents upstream breaking changes. The tag is only updated after the new Malcolm release has been tested with NetTap.

docs.title: Node.js Dependencies
docs.text: Node.js dependencies are managed via web/package.json with a lockfile (package-lock.json) for reproducible builds.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: NetTap uses pytest for the Python daemon and Vitest for the web dashboard. All tests must pass before a PR can be merged.

docs.title: Running All Tests
docs.text:
# Run everything
cd daemon && python -m pytest && cd ../web && npx vitest run && npx svelte-check

docs.title: Running

cd daemon

# Run all tests
python -m pytest tests/ -v

# Run with coverage
python -m pytest tests/ -v --cov=. --cov-report=term-missing

# Run a specific test file
python -m pytest tests/test_storage.py -v

# Run a specific test

daemon/tests/
