  test_smart.py           SmartMonitor unit tests
  test_api_server.py      API endpoint tests
  test_traffic.py         Traffic analysis tests
  test_alerts.py          Alert management tests
  test_devices.py         Device inventory tests
  ...

docs.title: Writing Daemon Tests
docs.text:
Tests use pytest fixtures to mock external dependencies (OpenSearch, disk I/O, SMART data):

Example test pattern
import pytest
from unittest.mock import MagicMock, patch
from storage.manager import StorageManager, RetentionConfig


@pytest.fixture
def mock_config():
    return RetentionConfig(
        hot_days=90,
        warm_days=180,
        cold_days=30,
        disk_threshold=0.80,
        emergency_threshold=0.90,
    )


@pytest.fixture
def mock_storage(mock_config):
    with patch("storage.manager.OpenSearch") as mock_os:
        storage = StorageManager(mock_config, "http://localhost:9200")
        yield storage


def test_disk_threshold(mock_storage):
    """Storage manager should trigger pruning above threshold."""
    # ... test implementation

docs.title: Key Testing Patterns
docs.text:
• Mock OpenSearch --- never connect to a real cluster in tests
  • Mock disk I/O --- use unittest.mock.patch for shutil.disk_usage
  • Mock SMART --- provide canned smartctl output
  • Test error handling --- verify behavior when OpenSearch is unreachable, disk is full, etc.
  • Test query building --- verify that API parameters produce correct OpenSearch queries

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
cd web

# Run all tests
npx vitest run

# Run in watch mode (re-runs on file changes)
npx vitest

# Run a specific test file
npx vitest run src/lib/components/TimeSeriesChart.test.ts

# Run with coverage
npx vitest run --coverage

docs.title: Type Checking
docs.text:
cd web

# Run svelte-check for TypeScript errors
npx svelte-check

docs.title: Test Structure
docs.text:
Tests are co-located with their source files using .test.ts or .spec.ts suffixes:

web/src/
  lib/
    components/
      TimeSeriesChart.svelte
      TimeSeriesChart.test.ts     # Component test
  api/
    traffic.ts
    traffic.test.ts               # API client test

docs.title: API Client Tests
docs.text:
Test that API client functions construct correct requests and handle responses:

Example API test
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { getTrafficSummary } from './traffic';

describe('getTrafficSummary', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.restoreAllMocks();
  });

  it('fetches traffic summary with default params', async () => {
    const mockResponse = { total_bytes: 1000, connection_count: 50 };
    global.fetch = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({
      ok: true,
      json: () => Promise.resolve(mockResponse),
    });

    const result = await getTrafficSummary();
    expect(result).toEqual(mockResponse);
    expect(fetch).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.stringContaining('/api/traffic/summary'),
      expect.anything()
    );
  });

  it('handles API errors gracefully', async () => {
    global.fetch = vi.fn().mockRejectedValue(new Error('Network error'));
    await expect(getTrafficSummary()).rejects.toThrow('Network error');
  });
});

docs.title: Component Tests
docs.text:
Test component rendering with mock data using Vitest and Testing Library:

Example component test
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/svelte';
import MyComponent from './MyComponent.svelte';

describe('MyComponent', () => {
  it('renders with data', () => {
    render(MyComponent, { props: { data: mockData } });
    expect(screen.getByText('Expected Text')).toBeInTheDocument();
  });

  it('shows loading state', () => {
    render(MyComponent, { props: { loading: true } });
    expect(screen.getByTestId('skeleton')).toBeInTheDocument();
  });

  it('shows empty state', () => {
    render(MyComponent, { props: { data: [] } });
    expect(screen.getByText('No data available')).toBeInTheDocument();
  });
});

docs.title: Key Testing Patterns
docs.text:
• Mock fetch --- never make real API calls in tests
  • Test all states --- loading, data, empty, error
  • Test interactions --- click handlers, form submissions
  • Test accessibility --- keyboard navigation, ARIA attributes

docs.title: Shell Script Linting
docs.text:
# Lint all shell scripts
shellcheck scripts/**/*.sh

# Lint a specific script
shellcheck scripts/install/install.sh

ShellCheck catches common shell scripting errors like unquoted variables, missing error handling, and portability issues.

docs.title: CI Integration
docs.text:
All tests run automatically in GitHub Actions on every push and PR:

  1. Python tests: cd daemon && python -m pytest
  2. Web tests: cd web && npx vitest run
  3. Type checking: cd web && npx svelte-check
  4. Shell linting: shellcheck scripts/**/*.sh

A PR cannot be merged until all CI checks pass.

docs.title: Test Coverage Requirements
docs.text:
• New features must include tests for both the daemon API layer and the web UI layer
  • Bug fixes should include a regression test that would have caught the bug
  • Daemon tests must mock OpenSearch (never connect to a real cluster)
  • Web tests must mock fetch (never make real API calls)
  • Component tests must cover loading, data, empty, and error states

docs.title: v1.0 Release Verification
docs.text: NetTap includes an automated release verification script that checks code quality, tests, and build integrity.

docs.title: Quick Check (CI-friendly)
docs.text:
Runs secrets audit, linting, tests, and type checking (~2-5 minutes):

cd ~/NetTap
./scripts/verify-release.sh --quick

docs.title: Full Verification
docs.text:
Includes Docker builds, Trivy CVE scanning, and E2E tests (~15-30 minutes):

cd ~/NetTap
./scripts/verify-release.sh --full

docs.title: Other Modes
docs.text:
# Secrets audit only
./scripts/verify-release.sh --secrets-only

# Quick checks + Docker builds
./scripts/verify-release.sh --docker

# Quick checks + Docker builds + Trivy scan
./scripts/verify-release.sh --trivy

# Verbose output (show full command output)
./scripts/verify-release.sh --quick -v

docs.title: Deployment Verification (Target Hardware)
docs.text: These commands verify a full deployment on reference hardware (Intel N100 or similar).

docs.title: 1. Clean Install
docs.text:
# On target host — fresh install
cd /opt/nettap
sudo scripts/install/install.sh

# Verify all containers are healthy
sudo docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}"

docs.title: 2. Container Health Checks
docs.text:
# Check each core service is responding
curl -sf http://localhost:8880/api/health | python3 -m json.tool        # Daemon API
curl -sk https://localhost:443/ -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n"   # Web dashboard
curl -sf http://localhost:9200/_cluster/health | python3 -m json.tool   # OpenSearch

docs.title: 3. Dashboard Load Timing
docs.text:
Target: page loads in < 3 seconds on LAN.

# Measure full page load time
curl -sk -o /dev/null -w "Total: %{time_total}s\nTTFB: %{time_starttransfer}s\n" https://localhost:443/

docs.title: 4. Bridge Throughput
docs.text:
Target: 500Mbps sustained with zero packet loss.

# On a machine behind the bridge, run iperf3 against the router/upstream
# Server side (on router or upstream machine):
iperf3 -s

# Client side (on machine behind bridge):
iperf3 -c <router-ip> -t 60 -P 4
# Expect: ~500+ Mbps, 0% packet loss

docs.title: 5. Alert Latency Test
docs.text:
Target: Suricata alerts appear in < 10 seconds.

# Trigger a known ET rule (e.g., ICMP to external host)
ping -c 1 8.8.8.8

# Check for alert in OpenSearch (within 10 seconds)
curl -sf 'http://localhost:9200/arkime_sessions3-*/_search?size=1&sort=@timestamp:desc&q=event.provider:suricata' \
  | python3 -m json.tool | head -20

docs.title: 6. Storage Pruning Verification
docs.text:
Target: daemon prunes at 80% disk threshold.

# Check current disk usage and daemon pruning config
curl -sf http://localhost:8880/api/storage/status | python3 -m json.tool

# View daemon logs for pruning activity
sudo docker logs nettap-storage-daemon 2>&1 | grep -i prune | tail -10

docs.title: First-run setup wizard
docs.text:
The setup wizard is now covered step by step in the setup guide:

  • Run the setup wizard: every step for each capture mode, with the defaults.
  • Go live: moving the cables in bridge mode, or switching your devices over in DHCP gateway mode.

docs.title: Hardware Guide
docs.text: This page covers compatible hardware, a reference build, and guidance for selecting components.

docs.title: Reference Build (~$200)
docs.text:
The target platform for NetTap is an Intel N100 mini PC. These are widely available, power-efficient, and provide excellent performance for network analysis workloads.

Component Specification Approx. Cost Mini PC Intel N100 (4-core, 3.4GHz boost), dual Intel i226-V 2.5GbE NICs $120--160 RAM 16 GB DDR4/DDR5 (often included) Included or $25 Storage 1 TB NVMe M.2 SSD $50--70 Total ~$200

Why the Intel N100?

The N100 is a 6W TDP processor that runs fanless in many mini PC designs. It has 4 cores (enough for Zeek + Suricata + OpenSearch), hardware AES-NI for TLS processing, and many mini PC vendors ship boards with dual Intel i226-V 2.5GbE ports already installed.

docs.title: CPU
docs.text:
NetTap needs to run Zeek, Suricata, OpenSearch, and several supporting containers simultaneously. Key considerations:

  • Minimum: 2 cores, x86-64 architecture
  • Recommended: 4 cores (Intel N100, N95, Celeron J4125, or better)
  • Ideal: Intel with AES-NI support (all modern Intel CPUs have this)

The CPU must be x86-64. ARM processors are not supported.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
OpenSearch is the largest memory consumer. The default JVM heap is 4 GB, and the full stack uses approximately 8--12 GB total.

  • 8 GB: Minimum. Works but may trigger OOM under heavy load.
  • 16 GB: Recommended. Comfortable headroom for all services.
  • 32 GB: Overkill for most home networks, but useful if you plan to increase OpenSearch heap size for larger datasets.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
NVMe SSDs are strongly recommended for both performance and endurance:

  • Read performance: OpenSearch performs many random reads during queries.
  • Write endurance: Zeek generates 300--800 MB of logs per day. NetTap includes write coalescing (30-second flush intervals) and SMART monitoring to protect drive life.
  • Capacity: A 1 TB drive comfortably holds 90 days of Zeek metadata, 180 days of Suricata alerts, and 30 days of PCAP captures for a typical home network.

SSD Write Endurance

A typical consumer 1 TB NVMe SSD is rated for 600 TBW (terabytes written). At 1 GB/day of log writes, NetTap would use about 365 GB/year --- meaning the drive would last many years. NetTap monitors SMART health and alerts you before drive failure.

docs.title: Network Interfaces
docs.text:
You need at least two physical Ethernet NICs for the data-path bridge. A third interface for management access is strongly recommended.

Recommended NICs:

NIC Speed Notes Intel i226-V 2.5 GbE Best choice. Common on N100 mini PCs. Excellent Linux support. Intel i225-V 2.5 GbE Previous generation. Works well but has known errata on early revisions. Intel I350 1 GbE Server-grade. Reliable but limited to 1 Gbps. Realtek RTL8125 2.5 GbE Works but Intel is preferred for packet capture workloads. Realtek RTL8111 1 GbE Budget option. Functional but lower performance under sustained capture.

NICs to avoid:

  • USB Ethernet adapters (unreliable for sustained capture)
  • Wi-Fi adapters (cannot be used for the bridge --- bridging requires wired Ethernet)
  • Virtual NICs (veth, tun/tap)

docs.title: Management Interface Options
docs.text:
The management interface is how you access the NetTap dashboard. Options:

  1. Third Ethernet NIC --- Most reliable. Assign a static IP or use DHCP.
  2. Wi-Fi adapter --- Convenient for mini PCs with built-in Wi-Fi. Less reliable than wired.
  3. VLAN on the LAN NIC --- Advanced. Requires VLAN-aware router configuration.

docs.title: Recommended Mini PCs
docs.text:
These models are known to work well with NetTap. All feature dual Intel i226-V 2.5GbE NICs:

Model CPU RAM Storage NICs Price Range Beelink EQ12 Pro Intel N100 16 GB 500 GB SSD 2x i226-V $150--180 Topton N100 Firewall Intel N100 16 GB 256 GB SSD 4x i226-V $140--170 CWWK N100 Intel N100 16 GB 256 GB SSD 2x i226-V $120--150 MinisForum UM560 AMD R5 5625U 16 GB 512 GB SSD 1x + USB $250--300

Community hardware reports

See the Hardware Compatibility reference for community-tested hardware reports. If you get NetTap running on hardware not listed here, please open a GitHub issue or PR to add your configuration.

docs.title: Cabling
docs.text:
ISP Modem ──[Ethernet]──> [WAN Port] NetTap [LAN Port] ──[Ethernet]──> Router WAN Port
                                        │
                                  [Management Port]
                                        │
                                  [Your LAN / Switch]
  1. Disconnect the Ethernet cable between your modem and router.
  2. Connect the modem to the NetTap WAN port.
  3. Connect the NetTap LAN port to your router's WAN port.
  4. Connect the management port to a switch or directly to your computer.

docs.title: Power and Placement
docs.text:
• Place NetTap physically between your modem and router (near your network "edge").
  • Use a UPS or battery backup if possible --- a power loss will interrupt the bridge and drop all network traffic until NetTap boots back up.
  • Ensure adequate ventilation. Fanless mini PCs can throttle under sustained load if airflow is restricted.

docs.title: Performance Expectations
docs.text:
With the reference Intel N100 build:

Metric Expected Performance Bridge latency < 1 ms added Sustained throughput 500 Mbps with zero packet loss Peak throughput Up to 1 Gbps (may see minor packet loss at sustained line rate) Dashboard load time < 3 seconds on LAN Alert detection latency < 10 seconds from packet to dashboard Power consumption 10--15W idle, 20--25W under load

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
This page is the reference for the install script: what each step does and every option. For a start-to-finish walkthrough, including choosing a capture mode and the setup wizard, follow the setup guide.

Which mode?

Mirror / SPAN is the recommended mode and the only one tested on real hardware so far. DHCP gateway is being tested, and inline bridge hasn't been verified with the current build. See choose how NetTap connects.

Mirror and DHCP gateway modes

Run the installer with --skip-bridge in mirror and DHCP gateway modes. Without it, the installer joins two ports into a bridge, and a bridged port loses its IP address, which can cut off your SSH session and the box's internet mid-install. The two-phase workflow below is for inline bridge mode.

In inline bridge mode, NetTap uses a two-phase workflow: Install (with internet, bridge activates automatically) → Rewire (physical cables, traffic flows immediately). The bridge activates during install with no cables — it sits idle until you plug in. This means you never lose your management connection.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting, ensure you have:

  • Ubuntu Server 22.04 or 24.04 LTS installed
  • Root or sudo access
  • At least two physical Ethernet NICs (three recommended for a dedicated management interface)
  • Internet access (to pull Docker images)
  • At least 20 GB of free disk space for Docker images

See Requirements for full details.

docs.title: Step 1: Clone the Repository
docs.text:
Clone into the home folder of the nettap user. NetTap's helper scripts in scripts/remote/ expect /home/nettap/NetTap:

cd ~
git clone https://github.com/EliasMarine/NetTap.git
cd ~/NetTap
git checkout v0.4.0-alpha.1

git checkout v0.4.0-alpha.1 pins the tested pre-release. Leave it out to install the latest main.

The installer generates every password, secret and certificate it needs (in docker/.env, docker/certs/, docker/ssl/, docker/curlrc/ and docker/auth/), and records your port roles in the repo-root .env. There's no separate secrets step. Don't copy .env.example to .env: the installer would skip asking which port is which. The one exception, for inline bridge mode with a wired management port, is in the setup guide.

docs.title: Step 2: Run the Installer
docs.text:
sudo scripts/install/install.sh

The installer will first run NIC discovery, which detects your physical network interfaces and lets you assign them to roles:

==========================================
  NetTap Pre-Install NIC Discovery
==========================================

Detected 3 physical network interface(s):

  #     Interface       Driver       Speed        MAC                  Link
  ---   -----------     ---------    ----------   ------------------   --------
  1     enp1s0          igc          2500Mb/s     aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01    link up  <-- current internet
  2     enp2s0          igc          2500Mb/s     aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:02    no link
  3     enp3s0          igc          2500Mb/s     aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:03    no link

Blink a NIC's LEDs to identify its port? (y/n): y
Enter NIC number (1-3): 1
Blinking enp1s0 for 10 seconds... look for the flashing port.

Select MANAGEMENT NIC (dashboard access): 1  [enp1s0]
Select WAN NIC (ISP modem side): 2  [enp2s0]
Select LAN NIC (router side): 3  [enp3s0]

Written to .env: MGMT=enp1s0, WAN=enp2s0, LAN=enp3s0

Then the installer runs through its steps automatically:

Step What It Does NIC preflight Discovers NICs, assigns MGMT/WAN/LAN roles, writes to .env 1. Pre-flight Validates root access, OS version, architecture, and hardware (CPU, RAM, disk, NICs) 2. Dependencies Installs Docker, bridge-utils, net-tools, ethtool, smartmontools, Python 3, Avahi 3. Kernel tuning Sets vm.max_map_count=262144 (required by OpenSearch), increases network buffer sizes 4. Bridge setup Creates the transparent br0 bridge between WAN and LAN NICs (no cables needed yet) 5. Malcolm deploy Pulls Malcolm container images (a spinner per image on a terminal), generates TLS certificates, and starts services 6. Systemd Installs and enables nettap.service for automatic start on boot 7. mDNS Configures Avahi so the dashboard is accessible at nettap.local 8. Firewall Adds UFW rules for the dashboard port, Malcolm port, and mDNS (if UFW is active) 9. Verification Checks the bridge, Docker, containers, OpenSearch, systemd, mDNS and kernel tuning, then prints the summary card

On a terminal, the installer shows the NetTap logo and a "Before we start" card (your WAN and LAN ports with their cable state, the dashboard address, and what happens to the bridge), then each step as [N/9] with a progress bar and ✓ / ! / ✗ check lines. Unless you pass --non-interactive, it then waits 5 seconds: Enter starts at once, Ctrl-C cancels. When the output is piped or logged it keeps the plain [NetTap] <timestamp> lines with no colour; force either look with sudo NETTAP_COLOR=never scripts/install/install.sh or NETTAP_COLOR=always. If a step fails, the installer names the step (for example "Install stopped at step 1/9: Pre-flight checks"), gives a hint, and prints the same command to run again.

At the end, the installer prints a summary card with the rewiring steps:

  ┃ NetTap is installed
  ┃
  ┃ Dashboard   https://nettap.local
  ┃ Malcolm     https://localhost:9443  on this box
  ┃ Checks      6 passed, 1 warning, 0 failed
  ┃ Time taken  14m 32s
  ┃
  ┃ Last step: move the cables
  ┃   1. ISP modem ──▸ enp2s0 (WAN)
  ┃   2. enp3s0 (LAN) ──▸ your router's WAN port
  ┃   3. Keep enp1s0 (MGMT) connected for the dashboard
  ┃
  ┃   Modem ──▸ enp2s0 ━━ NetTap ━━ enp3s0 ──▸ Router
  ┃   The bridge is on, so traffic flows as soon as both cables are in.
  ┃
  ┃ Manage      systemctl {start|stop|restart} nettap
  ┃ Logs        journalctl -u nettap -f
  ┃ Containers  docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml ps

No additional commands are needed — just plug in the cables and traffic flows.

docs.title: Installer Options
docs.text:
sudo scripts/install/install.sh [OPTIONS]
Option Description --defer-bridge Defer bridge activation until after cable rewiring (requires activate-bridge.sh) --non-interactive Auto-assign NICs without prompts. Needs three or more NICs: on a two-NIC box with internet it gives the internet NIC to management, has none left for LAN, and stops with "Could not assign WAN and LAN NICs", even with --skip-bridge (known bug). Run without it there --reconfigure-nics Force NIC re-discovery even if .env has values --skip-bridge Skip bridge configuration entirely --skip-pull Skip Docker image pull (use cached images) --skip-malcolm Skip Malcolm deployment entirely (deps only) --no-persist-bridge Don't write persistent netplan config (runtime-only bridge) --dry-run Log all actions without executing them -v, --verbose Enable debug output

docs.title: Phase 2: Rewire (physical cables)
docs.text:
After the installer completes, physically rewire your cables according to the diagram printed at the end of installation. The bridge is already active, so traffic flows immediately when both cables are connected:

  1. ISP modem → plug into the WAN NIC
  2. LAN NIC → plug into the router's WAN port
  3. Keep the MGMT NIC (or Wi-Fi) connected for dashboard access

Wi-Fi downtime is only the ~30 seconds it takes to physically swap two cables.

Identifying ports

During NIC discovery, you can blink a NIC's LEDs to identify which physical port it corresponds to. If you missed this step, run: 

sudo ethtool -p enp1s0 10
This blinks the LEDs on enp1s0 for 10 seconds. It doesn't work on every chip (Intel i226-V on Ubuntu's 6.8 kernel doesn't). Run ip -br link, plug in a cable, and run it again: the port that changes to UP is the one you plugged in.

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
After rewiring, you should see all services running:

docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml ps

OpenSearch not responding yet

The installer's own OpenSearch check doesn't sign in, so it often reports "OpenSearch not responding yet" even when all is well. Check with NetTap's login instead. "status" should be green or yellow: 

sudo docker exec nettap-opensearch curl --config /var/local/curlrc/.opensearch.primary.curlrc --cacert /usr/share/opensearch/config/certs/ca.crt --insecure -s 'https://localhost:9200/_cluster/health'
If it says Unauthorized, run bash scripts/remote/fix-opensearch.sh from ~/NetTap.

docs.title: Access the Dashboard
docs.text:
Open a browser and navigate to:

https://nettap.local

Or use the management IP directly:

https://192.168.1.100

Self-signed certificate

The first time you access the dashboard, your browser will warn about a self-signed TLS certificate. This is expected --- accept the warning to proceed. See TLS Certificates to configure a custom certificate.

If this is a fresh installation, you will be redirected to the setup wizard. The setup guide walks through it.

docs.title: Managing the Service
docs.text:
After installation, NetTap runs as a systemd service:

# Start all NetTap containers
sudo systemctl start nettap

# Stop all containers gracefully
sudo systemctl stop nettap

# Restart
sudo systemctl restart nettap

# Check status
systemctl status nettap

# View logs
journalctl -u nettap -f

NetTap starts automatically on boot. To disable auto-start:

sudo systemctl disable nettap

docs.title: Re-running NIC Discovery
docs.text:
If you need to change NIC assignments after installation:

sudo scripts/install/preflight.sh --reconfigure-nics

Or during a full re-install:

sudo scripts/install/install.sh --reconfigure-nics

docs.title: Deferred Bridge Mode (Advanced)
docs.text:
If you prefer the old three-phase workflow (install → rewire → activate), use --defer-bridge:

sudo scripts/install/install.sh --defer-bridge

This defers bridge activation and service startup until you explicitly run:

sudo scripts/install/activate-bridge.sh

The activation script validates cable carrier status, creates the bridge, and starts all services. Options:

Option Description --force Skip cable carrier validation --skip-services Activate bridge only, don't start Docker services --dry-run Log actions without executing -v, --verbose Enable debug output

activate-bridge.sh is also useful for troubleshooting — if you need to re-create the bridge or restart services after the initial install.

docs.title: Uninstallation
docs.text:
These steps are for inline bridge mode only. In mirror and DHCP gateway modes, --teardown takes down the ports recorded as WAN and LAN, which can include your management port, and NetTap leaves network settings behind that set a fixed address and routing at boot. Reinstall Ubuntu instead. Reinstalling is also the only way to undo every system change in bridge mode.

To remove NetTap:

cd ~/NetTap

# Stop services
sudo systemctl stop nettap

# Remove systemd service
sudo systemctl disable nettap
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/nettap.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload

# Tear down the bridge
sudo scripts/bridge/setup-bridge.sh --teardown

# Remove Docker containers and volumes (WARNING: deletes all data)
sudo docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml down -v

# Remove kernel tuning
sudo rm /etc/sysctl.d/99-nettap.conf
sudo sysctl --system

# Remove the installation directory
cd ~
sudo rm -rf ~/NetTap

Data loss

The docker compose down -v command deletes all Docker volumes, including OpenSearch data, PCAP captures, and Grafana dashboards. Back up any data you need before running this.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This page has moved into the setup guide, which covers the same ground in order and stays in step with the installer.

The short version, if you've done this before:

  1. Choose a mode: mirror (recommended), DHCP gateway (being tested) or inline bridge.
  2. Install Ubuntu Server 24.04 or 22.04 with the username nettap (section 3).
  3. git clone https://github.com/EliasMarine/NetTap.git into your home folder, git checkout v0.4.0-alpha.1, then from ~/NetTap run sudo scripts/install/install.sh. Add --skip-bridge for mirror and DHCP gateway modes. Inline bridge mode with a wired management port needs one extra step first (section 5).
  4. Open https://nettap.local and finish the wizard (section 6), then go live.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Before installing NetTap, make sure your hardware and software meet the following requirements.

docs.title: Minimum Specifications
docs.text:
Component Minimum Recommended CPU x86-64, 2 cores Intel N100 (4 cores) or equivalent RAM 8 GB 16 GB Storage 512 GB SSD 1 TB NVMe SSD Network 2 physical Ethernet NICs 2x Intel i226-V 2.5GbE + 1 management NIC Architecture x86-64 only ---

ARM is not supported

NetTap requires x86-64 architecture. ARM-based systems (Raspberry Pi, Apple Silicon, etc.) are not supported because the Malcolm stack's container images are built for x86-64 only.

docs.title: Network Interfaces
docs.text:
NetTap requires at least two physical Ethernet NICs for the transparent bridge:

  • WAN NIC --- connects to your ISP modem
  • LAN NIC --- connects to your router

A third interface (Ethernet, Wi-Fi, or USB) is strongly recommended for management access to the dashboard. Without it, you would need to access the dashboard from the router side of the bridge.

Why two NICs?

NetTap creates a Layer 2 bridge between the WAN and LAN interfaces. All traffic passes through transparently while NetTap captures a copy for analysis. The bridge interfaces have no IP addresses --- they are invisible on the network.

docs.title: Storage Considerations
docs.text:
NetTap stores network metadata, IDS alerts, and packet captures. Storage needs depend on your network activity:

Data Type Daily Size Default Retention 90-Day Total Zeek metadata (hot tier) 300--800 MB 90 days 27--72 GB Suricata alerts (warm tier) 10--50 MB 180 days 1.8--9 GB PCAP captures (cold tier) Variable 30 days Variable

An NVMe SSD is strongly recommended for write endurance and performance. NetTap includes SMART monitoring to track drive health.

docs.title: Operating System
docs.text:
OS Status Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS Fully supported Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS Supported Other Ubuntu versions May work, not tested Debian, Fedora, Arch, etc. Not supported

Why Ubuntu?

NetTap uses netplan for persistent bridge configuration, systemd for service management, and apt for package installation. These are all Ubuntu-native tools. Other distributions may work with modifications, but are not officially supported.

docs.title: Installed Automatically
docs.text:
The installation script installs all of these automatically. You do not need to install them manually:

  • Docker and Docker Compose v2
  • bridge-utils, net-tools, ethtool
  • smartmontools (SSD health monitoring)
  • Python 3.10+ and pip
  • avahi-daemon (mDNS for nettap.local access)
  • curl, jq, openssl

docs.title: Physical Setup
docs.text:
ISP Modem ──── [WAN NIC] ── NetTap ── [LAN NIC] ──── Router ──── Your devices
                                         │
                                   [Management NIC]
                                         │
                                    Dashboard access

docs.title: Ports Used
docs.text: Port Service Exposure 443 NetTap dashboard (HTTPS) Management interface only 80 HTTP redirect to HTTPS Management interface only 9443 Malcolm dashboards (HTTPS) Management interface only 8880 Daemon API (HTTP) Internal only (container-to-container) 9200 OpenSearch Loopback only (127.0.0.1) 5353/udp mDNS (Avahi) LAN broadcast

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text: If UFW is active on the host, the installer automatically adds rules for the dashboard port, Malcolm port, and mDNS. See the Firewall Configuration section for details.

docs.title: Pre-Installation Checklist
docs.text:
Before starting installation, confirm:

  • [ ] Hardware meets minimum specs (2+ cores, 8+ GB RAM, 512+ GB storage)
  • [ ] Two physical Ethernet NICs are installed and detected by the OS
  • [ ] Ubuntu Server 22.04 or 24.04 is installed (minimal server install is fine)
  • [ ] You have root or sudo access
  • [ ] The system has internet access (to pull Docker images)
  • [ ] The two data-path NICs are not assigned IP addresses (the installer handles this)

docs.title: Setup guide
docs.text:
This guide takes you from a new mini PC to a NetTap dashboard full of live data. It covers every step in order: picking hardware, choosing how NetTap joins your network, installing Ubuntu, running the installer and the setup wizard, and checking it all works. It finishes with updating, troubleshooting and removing NetTap.

You don't need to be a networking expert. You do need to be happy typing commands into a terminal and plugging cables into a router.

Pre-release. The current version is v0.4.0-alpha.1, the first alpha for early testers. Use mirror / SPAN mode: it's the one tested on real hardware. Expect rough edges, and keep a way to put your network back the way it was (see section 12).

Contents

  1. Before you start
  2. Choose how NetTap connects
  3. Install Ubuntu Server
  4. Get NetTap
  5. Run the installer
  6. Run the setup wizard
  7. Go live
  8. Check it works
  9. Find your way around
  10. Keep NetTap up to date
  11. Troubleshooting
  12. Take NetTap out of your network
  13. FAQ
  14. Going deeper

docs.title: What you'll end up with
docs.text: A small box on your network that records who talks to whom, flags threats with Suricata, keeps packet captures you can search, and shows it all at https://nettap.local. Everything stays on the box: no cloud account, no subscription.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Minimum Recommended CPU x86-64, 2 cores 4 cores, for example an Intel N100 RAM 8 GB 16 GB Disk 512 GB SSD 1 TB NVMe SSD Network ports 2 wired Ethernet ports 2 × 2.5 GbE ports, plus a third port or Wi-Fi for the dashboard

The installer stops if the box isn't x86-64, has fewer than 2 CPU cores, less than 8 GB of RAM or fewer than 2 network ports (Wi-Fi counts as one). It warns, but carries on, below 4 cores, 16 GB of RAM or about 400 GB of disk. ARM boards such as the Raspberry Pi aren't supported.

The installer checks for two ports even if you then pick a mode that uses only one.

docs.title: Hardware that has been tested
docs.text:
Box Network chips Ubuntu Mode tested GMKtec G11 (AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514) 2 × Realtek RTL8125BG 2.5 GbE 24.04.5 LTS Mirror / SPAN (November 2026 onwards) Intel N100 mini PC, 16 GB, 1 TB NVMe 2 × Intel i226-V 2.5 GbE 22.04 LTS Inline bridge, partly, on an older build (March 2026)

The install and the setup wizard were also tested from scratch on clean Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 virtual machines in November 2026, in mirror mode.

Other x86-64 boxes that meet the minimums should work. See the hardware guide for buying advice.

docs.title: You'll also need
docs.text:
• A USB stick (4 GB or more) to install Ubuntu.
  • A monitor and keyboard for the Ubuntu install. After that you can use SSH from another computer.
  • Ethernet cables: one or two more than you use today, depending on the mode.
  • Internet access during the install. NetTap downloads about 10 to 15 GB of container images.
  • For mirror mode only: a managed switch that can mirror a port (often called SPAN or port mirroring).

docs.title: How long it takes
docs.text: Allow about an hour from start to finish. The NetTap installer itself takes 10 to 20 minutes, most of it downloading, and the first data appears a few minutes after setup.

docs.title: 2. Choose how NetTap connects
docs.text:
Decide this first. It changes how you cable the box and how you run the installer, and it can't be changed in the app after setup yet.

Mirror / SPAN (recommended) DHCP gateway (being tested) Inline bridge (advanced) Network ports used 1 for capture, plus 1 for the dashboard 1 2 for the bridge, plus a 3rd port or Wi-Fi for the dashboard Extra hardware Managed switch with port mirroring None None Sees each device's own IP Yes Yes No, every device shows as your router's IP If NetTap stops or loses power Nothing happens to your network Devices lose internet until you turn your router's DHCP back on The bridge keeps forwarding if NetTap's services stop. A power cut or reboot drops the internet until the box is back up Tested on real hardware Yes Not yet Partly, on an older build Install command --skip-bridge --skip-bridge Default

Which one?

  • Recommended: mirror. If you have a managed switch, or can borrow one, pick mirror. It's the tested mode, it can't break your network, and it sees every device. The wizard marks it "Tested on hardware".
  • No managed switch, and you want per-device detail: DHCP gateway is being tested. It hasn't run on real hardware yet, and the wizard marks it "Not yet tested on hardware". Read its limits below, and only choose it if you're happy to help test it.
  • You want to see all internet traffic and have three ports (or two ports and Wi-Fi): inline bridge is under Advanced in the wizard. It ran on an N100 in March 2026, but the current build hasn't been verified with it. Devices behind your router all show up as the router's address.

docs.title: Mirror / SPAN (recommended)
docs.text:
Your managed switch sends NetTap a copy of the traffic on the port that connects the switch to your router. NetTap is outside the traffic path.

flowchart LR
    ISP[ISP modem] --- R[Your router]
    R --- S[Managed switch]
    S --- D[Your devices]
    S -- mirror port: a copy of the router port --> C[NetTap capture port]
    S --- M[NetTap management port<br/>dashboard]

The capture port gets no IP address. You reach the dashboard through the second port, which plugs into an ordinary switch port.

docs.title: DHCP gateway (being tested)
docs.text:
NetTap plugs into your router with one cable. It hands out addresses to your devices and passes their traffic on to the router, so it sees each device. You turn off your router's DHCP server as part of going live.

flowchart LR
    ISP[ISP modem] --- R[Your router<br/>DHCP turned off]
    R --- N[NetTap<br/>one port]
    R --- D[Your devices]
    D -. traffic goes via NetTap .-> N

Know these limits before you choose it:

  • Double NAT. Port forwards and UPnP on your router stop reaching your devices, and game consoles may report a strict NAT type.
  • IPv6 skips NetTap. If your router hands out IPv6 addresses, that traffic goes straight to the router. Turn IPv6 off on the router for full visibility.
  • Static IPs are invisible. Devices with a manually set IP address never use NetTap.
  • NetTap must stay on. If it's off, devices that got their address from NetTap lose internet until you turn the router's DHCP back on.

docs.title: Inline bridge (advanced)
docs.text:
NetTap sits between your modem and your router. The two bridge ports have no IP addresses. A third port, or Wi-Fi, gives you the dashboard.

flowchart LR
    ISP[ISP modem] --- W[NetTap WAN port]
    W === B((bridge))
    B === L[NetTap LAN port]
    L --- R[Your router]
    R --- D[Your devices]
    R --- M[NetTap management port<br/>or Wi-Fi]

Wi-Fi can be the management interface, but it can't be part of the bridge.

docs.title: 3. Install Ubuntu Server
docs.text:
NetTap runs on Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS or 22.04 LTS. Current testing is on 24.04. Follow Ubuntu's own server install tutorial. Only the choices below matter for NetTap.

Before you start the Ubuntu installer, plug in only one network cable:

Mode Plug in Mirror / SPAN The port you'll use for the dashboard, plugged into an ordinary port on your switch or router DHCP gateway The port that will connect to your router, plugged into your router Inline bridge The port you'll use for the dashboard, plugged into your router. Or skip the cable and set up Wi-Fi in the installer

Leave the other ports unplugged for now. You'll connect them in section 6 or section 7.

In the Ubuntu installer:

  1. Installation type: choose Ubuntu Server, not Ubuntu Server (minimized).
  2. Network: let the plugged-in port get its address automatically (DHCP).
  3. Storage: use the entire disk. Ubuntu's default LVM layout can leave much of a large disk unused, so on the summary screen check the size of ubuntu-lv. If it's smaller than the disk, edit it to the maximum size.
  4. Profile: use nettap as your username. NetTap's helper scripts expect the code at /home/nettap/NetTap. The server name doesn't matter, because the installer renames the box to nettap.
  5. SSH: tick Install OpenSSH server, so you can work from another computer.
  6. Featured server snaps: don't tick anything, especially not Docker. The NetTap installer installs Docker itself, and the snap version gets in its way.

When Ubuntu has rebooted, sign in as nettap (on the box or with ssh nettap@<the box's IP>) and bring it up to date:

sudo apt update

sudo apt upgrade -y

Check that the root filesystem has most of your disk:

df -h /
The size is much smaller than your disk

Grow the default Ubuntu volume to fill the disk. This only works with Ubuntu's default LVM layout:

sudo lvextend -r -l +100%FREE /dev/ubuntu-vg/ubuntu-lv

Then run df -h / again.

docs.title: Tell your ports apart
docs.text:
Ubuntu names ports things like enp1s0 and enp2s0. To see which name belongs to which socket, list them, plug a cable into one socket, and list them again:

ip -br link

The port you just plugged in changes from DOWN to UP. Write down which name is which. You'll need them in the installer and the wizard. The installer can also blink a port's light for you, though that doesn't work on every network chip.

docs.title: 4. Get NetTap
docs.text:
Ubuntu Server comes with git. Download NetTap into your home folder:

cd ~

git clone https://github.com/EliasMarine/NetTap.git

cd ~/NetTap

Switch to the tested pre-release, so your install matches what testers report against:

git checkout v0.4.0-alpha.1

Git says you're in a "detached HEAD" state. That's expected. Every command from here on runs from ~/NetTap (which is /home/nettap/NetTap) unless it says otherwise.

Don't copy .env.example to .env. The installer would then skip asking which port is which, and use the example's placeholder port names. Let the installer create .env, except in the one bridge-mode case in section 5.

docs.title: Pick the right command
docs.text:
Mode Command Mirror / SPAN sudo scripts/install/install.sh --skip-bridge DHCP gateway sudo scripts/install/install.sh --skip-bridge Inline bridge sudo scripts/install/install.sh

Why --skip-bridge matters: by default the installer joins two ports into a bridge, and a port in the bridge loses its IP address. In mirror and DHCP gateway modes that would take ports you need for something else. On a two-port box it always takes your management or router port, and with it your SSH session and the box's internet, partway through the download.

Bridge mode: the box must reach the internet through its management port or Wi-Fi during the install, never through the ports that become WAN or LAN. The bridge is built in step 4, before the downloads in step 5.

Bridge mode with a wired management port: one extra step first. The installer starts .env from .env.example, which gives the management port a fixed extra address, 192.168.1.100. That can clash with another device on your network. Start .env without the example's network lines instead:

grep -v -E '^(MGMT_|WAN_|LAN_)' .env.example > .env

The installer still asks about every port. Skip this step in mirror and DHCP gateway modes, and if you use Wi-Fi for management.

Run the command for your mode, for example in mirror mode:

sudo scripts/install/install.sh --skip-bridge

Run it as shown, without --non-interactive. On a box with exactly two ports, --non-interactive stops with "Could not assign WAN and LAN NICs" before it installs anything, even with --skip-bridge. This is a known bug: it gives your internet port to management and has no port left for LAN.

docs.title: Answer the port questions
docs.text:
First the installer lists your network ports. The one carrying your internet connection is marked <-- current internet. It offers to blink a port's light so you can find it.

  • Three or more ports: it asks for the MANAGEMENT port (dashboard access), then WAN (modem side), then LAN (router side). In bridge mode, choose the port marked <-- current internet (or your Wi-Fi) as MANAGEMENT. Never pick Wi-Fi as WAN or LAN.
  • Exactly two ports: it asks only for WAN and assigns LAN itself. It warns that there's no dedicated management port.
  • Mirror and DHCP gateway modes: these answers don't matter, because --skip-bridge means nothing is bridged. You pick the real ports in the setup wizard.

If you chose the internet port as WAN or LAN, it warns: "Internet will be unavailable until cables are rewired and bridge is activated." In bridge mode, press Ctrl-C and start again with the right ports.

docs.title: Let it run
docs.text:
The installer then shows a "Before we start" card and counts down from 5 seconds (Enter starts at once, Ctrl-C cancels). It works through nine steps:

Step What happens [1/9] Pre-flight checks Checks Ubuntu, CPU, RAM, disk and ports [2/9] Installing system dependencies Installs Docker, Compose, ethtool, smartmontools, Avahi and other packages [3/9] Applying kernel tuning Sets the kernel values OpenSearch and packet capture need [4/9] Configuring network bridge Builds the bridge br0 (skipped with --skip-bridge) [5/9] Deploying Malcolm stack Downloads the pinned Malcolm 26.10.0 images, builds NetTap's own images, generates passwords and certificates, starts everything [6/9] Installing systemd services Installs nettap.service so NetTap starts on boot [7/9] Configuring mDNS (nettap.local) Renames the box nettap and publishes nettap.local on your network [8/9] Configuring firewall rules Opens the dashboard and mDNS ports in UFW, if UFW is installed [9/9] Running post-install verification Checks the bridge, Docker, the containers, OpenSearch, mDNS and the boot service

Step 5 is the long one. It can sit for several minutes while OpenSearch and Logstash start. With --skip-bridge it may list the capture containers (zeek-live, suricata-live, pcap-capture) under "Some services are not healthy", because they don't know which port to capture on until you finish the wizard.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
A summary card that starts NetTap is installed and shows the dashboard address, https://nettap.local. In bridge mode it also tells you to move the cables. You can, but it's easier to wait: the Go live page walks you through it and keeps your internet up for longer.

With --skip-bridge the card still prints bridge cabling steps. Ignore them.

Two things in the output look wrong but aren't:

  • The warning "OpenSearch not responding yet" in the verification step. The installer's check doesn't sign in to OpenSearch, so it can't tell. Section 8 has the proper check.
  • The card's "Malcolm https://localhost:9443" line points at nothing. Malcolm's own dashboards are at https://nettap.local/dashboards/, behind the NetTap login.

If a step fails, the installer names it, gives a hint and prints the command to run again. Running the installer again is safe. It keeps the port roles, passwords and certificates it already made. To choose the ports again, add --reconfigure-nics.

All installer options Option What it does --skip-bridge Don't build the bridge (mirror and DHCP gateway modes) --defer-bridge Don't build the bridge or start NetTap yet. After moving the cables, run sudo scripts/install/activate-bridge.sh to do both --skip-pull Use container images already downloaded --skip-malcolm Do everything except download and start NetTap's containers --no-persist-bridge Build the bridge for this boot only --non-interactive Pick ports automatically, no questions. Needs three or more ports: on a two-port box it stops with "Could not assign WAN and LAN NICs" (known bug) --reconfigure-nics Ask about the ports again --dry-run Log the commands instead of running most of them. It still writes some system files, so it isn't a safe preview -v, --verbose More detail

sudo scripts/install/install.sh --help prints this list. The installation reference covers each step in more detail.

docs.title: Cable up first
docs.text: Mode Before you open the wizard Mirror / SPAN On your switch, mirror the port that connects it to your router (both directions) to a spare port. Plug NetTap's capture port into that spare port. Your switch's manual calls this port mirroring or SPAN DHCP gateway Nothing to do: the router port is already plugged into your router Inline bridge Nothing yet. Leave WAN and LAN unplugged until Go live

docs.title: Open the dashboard
docs.text:
On a computer or phone on the same network, open:

https://nettap.local

If that doesn't load, use the box's IP address instead. Run hostname -I on the box to find it.

Your browser warns that the certificate isn't trusted. That's expected: NetTap makes its own certificate. Accept the warning to continue. The TLS certificates page explains how to trust it or use your own.

Until an admin account exists, every page sends you to the setup wizard at /setup. Its steps depend on the mode:

Mode Steps DHCP gateway Welcome, Capture mode, Interfaces, DHCP gateway, Storage, Enrichment, Account, Verification Mirror / SPAN Welcome, Capture mode, Interfaces, Storage, Enrichment, Account, Verification Inline bridge Welcome, Capture mode, Interfaces, Bridge, Storage, Enrichment, Account, Verification

Nothing on your network changes until you select Complete setup on the Account step. In bridge and DHCP gateway modes, the real switch-over happens later, on Go live.

Welcome. Checks the network ports, the NetTap service and free disk space (100 GB or more). A failed check doesn't stop you, but fix it before you go on. Select Get started.

Capture mode. Pick the mode you chose in section 2: DHCP gateway, Mirror / SPAN, or Inline bridge (under Advanced).

Interfaces.

  • DHCP gateway: choose the router port, the port plugged into your router. If it warns the port has no IPv4 address, check the cable and select Refresh interfaces.
  • Mirror: choose the capture interface, the port plugged into the switch's mirror port. Leave the management interface on Auto-detect. The capture port must have no IP address and must not be your internet port. NetTap refuses it otherwise, and changes nothing.
  • Inline bridge: choose the WAN interface (modem side) and LAN interface (router side). Use the same ports you gave the installer.

DHCP gateway (DHCP gateway mode only). Pick the address range NetTap hands out. Keep the default, 10.77.0.0/24, unless your network already uses it. NetTap takes 10.77.0.1, keeps .2 to .9 free for devices with fixed addresses, and hands out .10 onwards.

Bridge (bridge mode only). Shows the planned bridge. Select Verify configuration, and don't skip it: it checks the plan without changing anything, and it saves your port choices for the Go Live page. It refuses a port the box still uses for its own connection.

Storage. How long NetTap keeps data, and when it starts deleting old data. The defaults suit most homes with a 1 TB disk:

Setting Default Hot tier (Zeek records and Suricata alerts) 90 days Warm tier 180 days Cold tier (packet captures) 30 days Warning threshold 80% disk Emergency threshold 90% disk

You can change these later in Settings › Retention.

Enrichment. If you use UniFi network gear, turn this on and add your controller's URL and an API key so NetTap can name your devices. Otherwise skip it. NetTap still works devices out from their traffic.

Account. Create the admin account you'll sign in with:

  • Username: at least 3 characters, using letters, numbers, - and _.
  • Password: at least 8 characters, with an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter and a number.

There's one admin account and no password reset in the app yet, so keep the password in a password manager. Select Complete setup. NetTap creates the account, signs you in and saves your capture settings. In mirror mode it starts capturing straight away.

Verification. Checks the NetTap service, OpenSearch, self-traffic exclusion, the bridge (bridge mode) and your UniFi controller (if you added one). A self-traffic warning doesn't stop anything. Then:

  • DHCP gateway and inline bridge: select Go Live setup.
  • Mirror: select Go to dashboard. You're done with setup; skip to section 8. (Don't use Go Live in mirror mode. That page is for the other two modes.)

docs.title: 7. Go live
docs.text: Use the same browser you ran the wizard in. In bridge mode, the Go Live page reads the ports that Verify configuration saved in that browser. Without them it shows the wrong port names.

docs.title: Inline bridge: move the cables
docs.text:
The page has three phases: Readiness, Wiring and Monitoring.

  1. Readiness checks the bridge and the ports.
  2. Wiring shows which cable goes where:
  3. Disconnect the cable from your ISP modem to your router.
  4. Connect the modem's cable to NetTap's WAN port.
  5. Connect a new cable from NetTap's LAN port to your router's WAN (internet) port.
  6. Wait for both ports to read Connected. The page moves on by itself.
  7. Monitoring shows the bridge carrying traffic.

Your internet is down only while you swap the cables. Keep the management port (or Wi-Fi) connected so you keep the dashboard.

docs.title: DHCP gateway: switch your devices over
docs.text:
1. Pre-checks. The page checks: network port connected, router found, router's DHCP server is off, address range is free, routing allowed, firewall ready, and IPv6 traffic. All but the IPv6 check must pass. The DHCP check fails at first, which is expected.
  2. Turn off your router's DHCP server.
  3. Open your router's admin page in a browser. The address and password are often on a sticker on the router. If you manage it with a phone app (most mesh systems), use the app.
  4. Find the DHCP server setting, usually under LAN, Network or Advanced.
  5. Turn the DHCP server off and save. Leave everything else as it is.
  6. Come back and select Check again.
  7. Turn on the DHCP gateway. Tick the box that says you understand NetTap becomes your network's gateway, then select Enable DHCP gateway.

  8. Restart NetTap once. This makes NetTap's address on your router's network permanent:

    sudo reboot

    When it's back, run the OpenSearch check in section 8. The page tells you to run the OpenSearch fix script after the restart. You only need it if the check fails. 5. Wait for devices to move over. Each device switches when its current address from the router runs out, which can take up to a day. To speed it up, turn a device's Wi-Fi off and on, or unplug and replug its cable.

The page also lists the devices that have a NetTap address, and has a Turn off DHCP server button and recovery steps if anything goes wrong. See devices lost internet.

docs.title: In the dashboard
docs.text: Open Home. Within about 5 minutes you should see devices, traffic and bandwidth. On the very first start, give it up to 15 minutes: OpenSearch and Logstash take a while.

docs.title: On the box
docs.text:
Every container should be up:

sudo docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}"

You should see about 15 nettap- containers. Most show Up … (healthy). nettap-zeek-live, nettap-suricata-live and nettap-pcap-capture have no health check and show just Up …. nettap-logstash can show (health: starting) for up to 10 minutes.

OpenSearch should accept NetTap's login:

sudo docker exec nettap-opensearch curl --config /var/local/curlrc/.opensearch.primary.curlrc --cacert /usr/share/opensearch/config/certs/ca.crt --insecure -s 'https://localhost:9200/_cluster/health'

Look for "status":"green" or "status":"yellow" in the reply. Yellow is normal on a single box. If it says Unauthorized instead, see the dashboard is empty.

NetTap should start on boot:

systemctl is-enabled nettap

It should print enabled.

Mirror mode: check the capture end to end

This script checks that the capture port has no IP address, is receiving other devices' traffic (proof the mirror works), will survive a reboot, and that every capture container is listening on it. It updates the code with git pull first.

bash scripts/remote/verify-mirror-mode.sh

docs.title: 9. Find your way around
docs.text:
The sidebar has four groups:

Group Pages Overview Home (headline numbers), Live Monitor (current connections, with a globe), Bandwidth Investigate Alerts, Threats, Connections, Log Explorer, DNS Analytics, Certificates, PCAP Search, Packet analysis, Investigations Devices Devices (each device's traffic, alerts and risk score), IoT & LAN, Changelog System Infrastructure, System, Security posture, Tools, Settings

Worth doing in your first week:

  • Settings › Notifications: get alerts by email, Discord, Slack, Telegram, Pushover or webhook. See notifications.
  • Settings › Network: set your location, so the Live Monitor globe draws traffic from your home.
  • Devices: give your devices names and pictures, so alerts make sense at a glance.

The user guide explains each page.

docs.title: 10. Keep NetTap up to date
docs.text:
What How Malcolm, Suricata rules, GeoIP data In the app: System › Software updates Ubuntu On the box: sudo apt update, then sudo apt upgrade NetTap itself Pull the new code and run the installer again (below)

In the app. System › Software updates lists what's out of date. NetTap backs up first and rolls back if an update fails. A Malcolm update takes 10 to 40 minutes, and you can leave the page while it runs. NetTap only offers Malcolm releases it has been tested with.

Ubuntu. The updates page shows a count of waiting Ubuntu updates. Security updates install themselves.

NetTap. NetTap can't replace itself from the updates page. Get the new code and run the installer again:

cd ~/NetTap

git pull

sudo scripts/install/install.sh

In mirror or DHCP gateway mode, add --skip-bridge to the last command, as you did the first time. The installer keeps your port roles, passwords and certificates, rebuilds NetTap's containers and keeps your data. This upgrade path hasn't yet been tested end to end before a release, so check section 8 afterwards.

See updating for more.

docs.title: I lost my connection during the install
docs.text:
Cause: the port you were using became part of the bridge. This happens in bridge mode if the internet port was picked as WAN or LAN, or in mirror or DHCP gateway mode if you left out --skip-bridge.

Fix: on the box's own screen and keyboard, remove the bridge and restart:

cd ~/NetTap

sudo scripts/bridge/setup-bridge.sh --teardown

sudo reboot

Ubuntu's own network settings bring the port back. Then run the installer again with the right command for your mode. Add --reconfigure-nics to choose the ports again.

docs.title: The dashboard is empty, or says Unauthorized
docs.text:
Cause: OpenSearch isn't accepting NetTap's login, so nothing gets stored or shown. NetTap's settings should keep the login working across restarts, but this hasn't been confirmed on every setup yet.

Fix: run the OpenSearch check. If it says Unauthorized, run the fix script from the NetTap folder:

cd ~/NetTap

bash scripts/remote/fix-opensearch.sh

It repairs the login, restarts the services that depend on it, and waits for them to come back. If it tells you to recreate OpenSearch once, run the command it prints, then run the script again.

docs.title: nettap.local doesn't open
docs.text: Some phones and Windows computers don't look up .local names. Use the box's IP address instead (hostname -I on the box shows it): https://<that address>.

docs.title: The browser says the connection isn't private
docs.text: Expected. NetTap signs its own certificate. Accept the warning, or follow TLS certificates to trust it.

docs.title: Containers stay on "starting"
docs.text:
Logstash can take up to 10 minutes on first start. Wait, then check again. If a container keeps restarting, look at its log:

sudo docker logs nettap-logstash --tail 50

Put the name of the failing container in place of nettap-logstash.

docs.title: The port light doesn't blink
docs.text: Not every network chip supports it. Intel i226-V ports on Ubuntu's 6.8 kernel don't. Use the plug-and-look method in Tell your ports apart instead.

docs.title: Mirror mode: no traffic shows up
docs.text:
• Check the switch: the mirror source should be the port connecting the switch to your router, both directions, and the destination should be NetTap's capture port.
  • The capture port must have no IPv4 address and must not be the internet port. Pick a spare one.
  • If the capture port has picked up an IPv6 address, restart its service:
sudo systemctl restart nettap-mirror.service

Then run bash scripts/remote/verify-mirror-mode.sh to see exactly what's wrong.

docs.title: Packet capture stopped
docs.text:
There are three possible causes:

  • The disk passed 95%. NetTap pauses capture and starts it again by itself once usage drops below 85%. Lower the retention days in Settings › Retention to free space sooner.
  • Capture is switched off in Settings › Capture. Switch it back on.
  • Something else stopped the capture container. Run the fix script. It restarts capture only if neither of the first two causes applies, and otherwise tells you which one does:
bash scripts/remote/fix-pcap-capture-stopped.sh

docs.title: DHCP gateway: devices lost internet
docs.text:
With NetTap down and your router's DHCP off, nothing hands out addresses.

  1. Turn your router's DHCP server back on. Give a laptop a fixed address on your router's network (plugged into the router, or on its Wi-Fi), open the router's admin page and turn DHCP on. With a phone-app router, use the app, on mobile data if your Wi-Fi has no internet.
  2. Reconnect your devices (Wi-Fi off and on, or unplug and replug). They get an address from the router straight away. Set the laptop back to automatic.
  3. When NetTap is healthy again, go back to Go Live to switch the gateway back on.

docs.title: I forgot the admin password
docs.text: There's no reset in the app yet. If you're stuck, open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: Something else
docs.text:
The troubleshooting reference covers more. For a bug, open an issue with the output of:

sudo docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}"

docs.title: 12. Take NetTap out of your network
docs.text:
Undo the wiring first. Your internet then works without NetTap.

  • Inline bridge: plug the modem's cable straight back into your router's WAN port.
  • Mirror: unplug NetTap. Turn off the mirror session on the switch if you like.
  • DHCP gateway:
    1. Turn your router's DHCP server back on.
    2. On Go Live, select Turn off DHCP server, then Yes, turn off DHCP server. The page then shows Hand your network back to the router.
    3. Reconnect your devices (Wi-Fi off and on, or unplug and replug) so they get an address from the router.
    4. Unplug NetTap.

To stop NetTap but keep it installed:

sudo systemctl disable --now nettap

To remove NetTap completely, reinstall Ubuntu on the box. There's no uninstall script, and NetTap changes more than its own folder. Mirror and DHCP gateway modes write network settings that set a fixed address and routing at every boot. The installation reference lists the manual steps for inline bridge mode.

docs.title: 13. FAQ
docs.text:
Will NetTap slow down my internet? In mirror mode, no: it only receives a copy. In bridge mode the Linux kernel forwards traffic itself, and NetTap is designed to add under 1 ms. Bridge throughput hasn't been benchmarked yet. In DHCP gateway mode, all device traffic passes through NetTap's one port.

Does my data leave the house? No. There's no cloud, no account and no telemetry. NetTap does use the internet for update checks, threat rule downloads, GeoIP data and WHOIS lookups.

Can NetTap see inside encrypted (HTTPS) traffic? No. It sees who each device talks to, the site names in the TLS handshake, certificates, sizes and timing, but not the content.

Can NetTap block traffic? No. This version only watches and reports.

How much disk does it use? Usually 300 to 800 MB of records a day, plus packet captures. Captures are kept for 30 days and use at most 25% of the disk. The daemon checks the disk every 5 minutes. At 80% it deletes data past its retention, at 90% it deletes the oldest captures and then the oldest records, and at 95% it also pauses capture until usage drops below 85%.

Can I change the mode later? Not from the app yet. Pick carefully in section 2.

Why does every device show as my router in bridge mode? The bridge sits outside your router, after it has translated every device's address to its own (NAT). For per-device detail, use mirror or DHCP gateway mode.

Can I run it on a Raspberry Pi or in a virtual machine? Not on a Pi: NetTap needs x86-64. A virtual machine gets a warning from the installer and hasn't been tested.

docs.title: NetTap Web UI v2 — Implementation Plan
docs.text:
For Claude: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task.

Goal: Complete redesign of the NetTap web UI as a guided power-user SIEM tool with Datadog/Grafana aesthetic, including new daemon API endpoints for log exploration, OpenSearch cluster visibility, and Logstash monitoring.

Architecture: SvelteKit frontend (keep infra: Docker, nginx, auth, adapter-node) with all pages rebuilt from scratch. Python aiohttp daemon gets 3 new API modules (logs, opensearch cluster, logstash). Frontend uses $lib/server/daemon.ts proxy to talk to daemon. All pages dark-themed with colorful data visualizations.

Tech Stack: SvelteKit 2 + Svelte 5, TypeScript, aiohttp (daemon), OpenSearch Python client, Vitest + Testing Library, pytest

Design Doc: docs/plans/2026-03-05-webui-v2-redesign.md

Mockups: Each page gets an HTML mockup in mockups/<page-name>/index.html for user approval before implementation. Use frontend-design skill for each mockup.

docs.title: Phase 0: Mockups (Approval Gate)
docs.text: Every page must be mocked up and approved before implementation begins. Mockups are standalone HTML files with inline CSS — no build step needed, just open in browser.

docs.title: Task 0.1: Dashboard Mockup
docs.text:
Files: - Create: mockups/dashboard-v2/index.html

What to mock: - Stat cards row: bandwidth, connections, alerts, devices, system health - Area chart: bandwidth over time (24h, 1h buckets) with gradient fill - Geo map placeholder: world map with connection dots - Protocol donut chart with legend - Top talkers horizontal bar chart - Alert trend sparkline (stacked by severity) - Dark theme, Datadog/Grafana colors: dark bg (#0d1117), vibrant chart colors - Auto-refresh indicator, time range selector

Use: frontend-design skill

docs.title: Task 0.2: Log Explorer Mockup
docs.text:
Files: - Create: mockups/log-explorer/index.html

What to mock: - Log type tabs/dropdown: Zeek conn, dns, http, tls, files, dhcp, smtp, Suricata, All - Search bar with field-aware placeholder text - Time range selector (presets + custom) - Column picker sidebar (checkboxes, drag to reorder) - Results table: sortable columns, monospace data, alternating row shading - Expandable row: click to show raw JSON + field tooltips - Field statistics panel: top 5 values for selected field - Pagination controls (cursor-based) - Export button (CSV/JSON) - Tooltips: hover any Zeek field name → plain-English description

docs.title: Task 0.3: Devices Mockup

# daemon/tests/test_logs_api.py
"""Tests for daemon/api/logs.py — generic Zeek/Suricata log search."""

import json
import unittest
from unittest.mock import MagicMock, patch
from aiohttp.test_utils import AioHTTPTestCase
from aiohttp import web
from api.logs import register_log_routes

class TestLogSearchAPI(AioHTTPTestCase):
    async def get_application(self):
        app = web.Application()
        storage = MagicMock()
        storage._client = MagicMock()
        register_log_routes(app, storage)
        return app

    async def test_search_default_params(self):
        """GET /api/logs/search returns results with default params."""
        with patch.object(
            self.app["storage"]._client, "search",
            return_value={"hits": {"hits": [], "total": {"value": 0}}}
        ):
            resp = await self.client.request("GET", "/api/logs/search")
            self.assertEqual(resp.status, 200)
            data = await resp.json()
            self.assertIn("hits", data)
            self.assertIn("total", data)

    async def test_search_by_log_type(self):
        """GET /api/logs/search?log_type=zeek.dns filters correctly."""
        with patch.object(
            self.app["storage"]._client, "search",
            return_value={"hits": {"hits": [], "total": {"value": 0}}}
        ) as mock_search:
            resp = await self.client.request("GET", "/api/logs/search?log_type=zeek.dns")
            self.assertEqual(resp.status, 200)
            call_body = mock_search.call_args[1]["body"]
            # Should have term filter for event.dataset=dns
            filters = call_body["query"]["bool"]["filter"]
            datasets = [f["term"]["event.dataset"] for f in filters if "event.dataset" in f.get("term", {})]
            self.assertIn("dns", datasets)

    async def test_search_with_query_string(self):
        """GET /api/logs/search?query=google.com uses query_string."""
        with patch.object(
            self.app["storage"]._client, "search",
            return_value={"hits": {"hits": [], "total": {"value": 0}}}
        ) as mock_search:
            resp = await self.client.request("GET", "/api/logs/search?query=google.com")
            self.assertEqual(resp.status, 200)
            call_body = mock_search.call_args[1]["body"]
            self.assertIn("query_string", json.dumps(call_body))

    async def test_search_pagination(self):
        """GET /api/logs/search?size=10 respects size param."""
        with patch.object(
            self.app["storage"]._client, "search",
            return_value={"hits": {"hits": [], "total": {"value": 0}}}
        ) as mock_search:
            resp = await self.client.request("GET", "/api/logs/search?size=10")
            self.assertEqual(resp.status, 200)
            call_body = mock_search.call_args[1]["body"]
            self.assertEqual(call_body["size"], 10)

    async def test_fields_endpoint(self):
        """GET /api/logs/fields/zeek.conn returns field list."""
        resp = await self.client.request("GET", "/api/logs/fields/zeek.conn")
        self.assertEqual(resp.status, 200)
        data = await resp.json()
        self.assertIn("fields", data)
        # Should have standard Zeek conn fields
        field_names = [f["name"] for f in data["fields"]]
        self.assertIn("source.ip", field_names)
        self.assertIn("destination.ip", field_names)

"""
NetTap Log Search API Routes

Generic log browser for Zeek and Suricata logs stored in OpenSearch.
Supports filtering by log type, full-text search, time range,
field projection, sorting, and cursor-based pagination.
"""

import logging
import os
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

from aiohttp import web
from opensearchpy import OpenSearchException

from storage.manager import StorageManager

logger = logging.getLogger("nettap.api.logs")

NETWORK_INDEX = os.environ.get("OPENSEARCH_NETWORK_INDEX", "arkime_sessions3-*")

# Log type → OpenSearch filter mapping
LOG_TYPE_FILTERS = {
    "zeek.conn": [{"term": {"event.provider": "zeek"}}, {"term": {"event.dataset": "conn"}}],
    "zeek.dns": [{"term": {"event.provider": "zeek"}}, {"term": {"event.dataset": "dns"}}],
    "zeek.http": [{"term": {"event.provider": "zeek"}}, {"term": {"event.dataset": "http"}}],
    "zeek.tls": [{"term": {"event.provider": "zeek"}}, {"term": {"event.dataset": "ssl"}}],
    "zeek.files": [{"term": {"event.provider": "zeek"}}, {"term": {"event.dataset": "files"}}],
    "zeek.dhcp": [{"term": {"event.provider": "zeek"}}, {"term": {"event.dataset": "dhcp"}}],
    "zeek.smtp": [{"term": {"event.provider": "zeek"}}, {"term": {"event.dataset": "smtp"}}],
    "suricata": [{"term": {"event.provider": "suricata"}}],

# Field definitions per log type (name, type, description, example)

    ],

# Default time range: last 24 hours
_DEFAULT_RANGE_HOURS = 24
_MAX_SIZE = 500
_DEFAULT_SIZE = 50


def _parse_time_range(request: web.Request) -> tuple[str, str]:
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    default_from = (now - timedelta(hours=_DEFAULT_RANGE_HOURS)).isoformat()
    default_to = now.isoformat()
    raw_from = request.query.get("from", "")
    raw_to = request.query.get("to", "")
    if raw_from:
        try:
            datetime.fromisoformat(raw_from.replace("Z", "+00:00"))
        except (ValueError, TypeError):
            raw_from = ""
    if raw_to:
        try:
            datetime.fromisoformat(raw_to.replace("Z", "+00:00"))
        except (ValueError, TypeError):
            raw_to = ""
    return (raw_from or default_from, raw_to or default_to)


async def handle_log_search(request: web.Request) -> web.Response:
    """GET /api/logs/search — Generic log search across Zeek/Suricata indices."""
    storage: StorageManager = request.app["storage"]
    from_ts, to_ts = _parse_time_range(request)

    log_type = request.query.get("log_type", "")
    query_str = request.query.get("query", "")
    fields = request.query.get("fields", "")
    size = min(int(request.query.get("size", _DEFAULT_SIZE)), _MAX_SIZE)
    sort_param = request.query.get("sort", "@timestamp:desc")
    search_after = request.query.get("search_after", "")

    # Build query
    filters = [{"range": {"@timestamp": {"gte": from_ts, "lte": to_ts}}}]

    if log_type and log_type in LOG_TYPE_FILTERS:
        filters.extend(LOG_TYPE_FILTERS[log_type])

    must = []
    if query_str:
        must.append({"query_string": {"query": query_str, "default_operator": "AND"}})

    body: dict = {
        "query": {"bool": {"must": must if must else [{"match_all": {}}], "filter": filters}},
        "size": size,
        "sort": [],
    }

    # Sort
    for part in sort_param.split(","):
        if ":" in part:
            field, order = part.split(":", 1)
            body["sort"].append({field: {"order": order}})
        else:
            body["sort"].append({part: {"order": "desc"}})
    # Always add _id tiebreaker for cursor pagination
    if not any("_id" in s for s in body["sort"]):
        body["sort"].append({"_id": {"order": "desc"}})

    # Cursor pagination
    if search_after:
        try:
            body["search_after"] = json.loads(search_after)
        except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError):
            pass

    # Field projection
    if fields:
        body["_source"] = [f.strip() for f in fields.split(",")]

    try:
        import asyncio
        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
        result = await loop.run_in_executor(
            None, lambda: storage._client.search(index=NETWORK_INDEX, body=body)
        )

        hits = result.get("hits", {})
        documents = []
        last_sort = None
        for hit in hits.get("hits", []):
            doc = hit.get("_source", {})
            doc["_id"] = hit.get("_id")
            doc["_index"] = hit.get("_index")
            documents.append(doc)
            last_sort = hit.get("sort")

        return web.json_response({
            "hits": documents,
            "total": hits.get("total", {}).get("value", 0),
            "search_after": last_sort,
            "size": size,
            "log_type": log_type or "all",
        })
    except OpenSearchException as exc:
        logger.exception("Log search failed")
        return web.json_response({"error": f"Search failed: {exc}"}, status=500)


async def handle_log_fields(request: web.Request) -> web.Response:
    """GET /api/logs/fields/{log_type} — Return field definitions for a log type."""
    log_type = request.match_info.get("log_type", "")

    if log_type not in FIELD_DEFINITIONS:
        return web.json_response(
            {"error": f"Unknown log type: {log_type}", "available": list(FIELD_DEFINITIONS.keys())},
            status=400,
        )

    return web.json_response({"log_type": log_type, "fields": FIELD_DEFINITIONS[log_type]})


import json

def register_log_routes(app: web.Application, storage: StorageManager) -> None:
    app["storage"] = storage
    app.router.add_get("/api/logs/search", handle_log_search)
    app.router.add_get("/api/logs/fields/{log_type}", handle_log_fields)
    logger.info("Log search API routes registered (2 endpoints)")

"""
NetTap OpenSearch Cluster API Routes

Provides cluster health, index listing, shard allocation, and template
information from the local OpenSearch instance.
"""

import asyncio
import logging

from aiohttp import web
from opensearchpy import OpenSearchException

from storage.manager import StorageManager

logger = logging.getLogger("nettap.api.opensearch_cluster")


async def handle_cluster_health(request: web.Request) -> web.Response:
    """GET /api/opensearch/cluster — Cluster health + stats."""
    storage: StorageManager = request.app["storage"]
    try:
        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
        health = await loop.run_in_executor(None, storage._client.cluster.health)
        stats = await loop.run_in_executor(None, lambda: storage._client.cluster.stats())
        return web.json_response({
            **health,
            "total_indices": stats.get("indices", {}).get("count", 0),
            "total_docs": stats.get("indices", {}).get("docs", {}).get("count", 0),
            "total_size_bytes": stats.get("indices", {}).get("store", {}).get("size_in_bytes", 0),
        })
    except OpenSearchException as exc:
        logger.exception("Failed to get cluster health")
        return web.json_response({"error": str(exc)}, status=500)


async def handle_indices(request: web.Request) -> web.Response:
    """GET /api/opensearch/indices — Index list with details."""
    storage: StorageManager = request.app["storage"]
    try:
        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
        indices = await loop.run_in_executor(
            None,
            lambda: storage._client.cat.indices(
                format="json",
                h="index,health,status,docs.count,store.size,pri.store.size,creation.date.string",
                s="index",
            )
        )
        return web.json_response({"indices": indices or [], "count": len(indices or [])})
    except OpenSearchException as exc:
        logger.exception("Failed to list indices")
        return web.json_response({"error": str(exc)}, status=500)


async def handle_shards(request: web.Request) -> web.Response:
    """GET /api/opensearch/shards — Shard allocation details."""
    storage: StorageManager = request.app["storage"]
    try:
        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
        shards = await loop.run_in_executor(
            None,
            lambda: storage._client.cat.shards(
                format="json",
                h="index,shard,prirep,state,docs,store,node",
                s="index,shard",
            )
        )
        return web.json_response({"shards": shards or [], "count": len(shards or [])})
    except OpenSearchException as exc:
        logger.exception("Failed to list shards")
        return web.json_response({"error": str(exc)}, status=500)


async def handle_templates(request: web.Request) -> web.Response:
    """GET /api/opensearch/templates — Index template list."""
    storage: StorageManager = request.app["storage"]
    try:
        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
        templates = await loop.run_in_executor(
            None,
            lambda: storage._client.cat.templates(
                format="json",
                h="name,index_patterns,order,version",
                s="name",
            )
        )
        return web.json_response({"templates": templates or [], "count": len(templates or [])})
    except OpenSearchException as exc:
        logger.exception("Failed to list templates")
        return web.json_response({"error": str(exc)}, status=500)


def register_opensearch_cluster_routes(app: web.Application, storage: StorageManager) -> None:
    app["storage"] = storage
    app.router.add_get("/api/opensearch/cluster", handle_cluster_health)
    app.router.add_get("/api/opensearch/indices", handle_indices)
    app.router.add_get("/api/opensearch/shards", handle_shards)
    app.router.add_get("/api/opensearch/templates", handle_templates)
    logger.info("OpenSearch cluster API routes registered (4 endpoints)")
