The apply proxy calls daemonFetch with the default 10_000 ms timeout. handle_apply_updates awaits ue.apply_update, which runs docker pulls and rule/GeoIP downloads with up to a 300 s timeout. On abort, daemonFetch returns 502, applyUpdates returns {state:'error', results:[]}, and handleApplyUpdates sets updateCompleted=true, so the title reads 'Update Complete' with no counts. The daemon never sends a 'state' field, and the 'already in progress' response is a 200 that also ends as Complete. aiohttp>=3.9 is pinned, which does not cancel handlers when the client disconnects.
  • Tracked: new
  • Issue: The daemon's POST /api/system/updates/apply awaits the whole update before it responds (docker image pulls, rule and GeoIP downloads). The web proxy calls daemonFetch with its default 10_000 ms timeout and returns 502 when it expires. applyUpdates() turns any non-2xx response into {state:'error', results:[]}. The page treats every state other than 'in_progress' as finished: it sets updateCompleted=true and the panel title reads "Update Complete", with no success or failure counts and no error text. The daemon runs aiohttp >= 3.9, which does not cancel handlers when the client disconnects, so the update keeps running. A second click gets a 200 response with "An update is already in progress", which also renders as "Update Complete". rollbackComponent failures are swallowed the same way.
  • Failure scenario: The user clicks Update on zeek/suricata. About 10 s later the panel says "Update Complete" while the daemon is still pulling and restarting capture containers. The user may reboot or start another update in the middle of the operation, and never sees per-component results or failures.
  • Fix: Make apply asynchronous in the daemon: start a task and return 202, and have the page poll /status (the client's status contract also has to match the daemon's {status, current_update}). Alternatively pass a long timeout for this proxy route. Make applyUpdates and rollbackComponent throw on !res.ok and on bodies containing "error", and show the error in the panel instead of "Update Complete". (effort M)

docs.title: CR-036 (HIGH) — Threats page shows a clean 'no threats' report when the threat analysis fails
docs.text:
• Where: web/src/routes/threats/+page.svelte:145
  • Verdict: CONFIRMED. getThreatReport (threats.ts:152) returns a report with score 0, level 'none' and empty lists on any !res.ok. fetchAll stores it as report = reportRes, so the '!report' error branch (line 213) runs only when an exception is thrown. daemon/api/threats.py:61 returns 500 when the report fails. The headline derives 'No actionable threats detected.' from total_groups 0.
  • Tracked: new
  • Issue: getThreatReport (web/src/lib/api/threats.ts:152) returns a made-up report with threat_score 0, threat_level 'none' and empty lists on any non-OK response. The page stores it as a real report (report = reportRes). So the 'Failed to load threat intelligence data.' branch at line 213 only runs on a network exception or a 30s timeout, never on an HTTP error. The daemon's handle_threat_report returns 500 when report generation fails, and the web proxy returns 502 or 401 when the daemon is down or the token is wrong.
  • Failure scenario: OpenSearch is overloaded and /api/threats/report returns 500, or the daemon is restarting and the proxy returns 502. The page shows THREAT SCORE 0, level NONE, 'No actionable threats detected.', 'No beaconing patterns detected.' and 'No lateral movement detected.' A security appliance reports an all-clear exactly when its analysis did not run.
  • Fix: Make getThreatReport and getThreatIntel throw on !res.ok, as PR #110 did for alerts/iot/live. The existing catch then sets report = null and the existing 'Failed to load' branch shows. (effort S)

docs.title: CR-038 (HIGH) — ISM policies match no real index and use rollover without an alias, so tiered retention never applies
docs.text:
• Where: config/opensearch/ilm-policy.json:92, config/opensearch/ilm-policy.json:93
  • Verdict: CONFIRMED. The ism_template patterns are zeek-, suricata- and arkime-/pcap-. Compose sets MALCOLM_NETWORK_INDEX_PATTERN arkime_sessions3-* and MALCOLM_OTHER_INDEX_PATTERN malcolm_beats_, and 'arkime-' does not match 'arkime_sessions3' (underscore). Every hot state starts with a rollover action on non-alias indices. daemon/storage/manager.py TIER_PREFIXES maps 'arkime' to cold (30d), so malcolm_beats* is unknown and is skipped by prune_oldest_indices.
  • Tracked: related to PR #144 follow-up: POST /api/ilm/apply applies the static policy out…
  • Issue: ism_template patterns are zeek-, suricata- and arkime-/pcap-. Malcolm writes all Zeek and Suricata data to arkime_sessions3-* (MALCOLM_NETWORK_INDEX_PATTERN) and other data to malcolm_beats_, so none of the patterns match. The hot state also starts with a rollover action, which fails on Malcolm's dated, non-alias indices, and ISM never reaches the delete transition. On the connected daemon side, storage/manager.py _TIER_PREFIXES maps every 'arkime' index to the cold tier (30d) and malcolm_beats_* to unknown.
  • Malcolm pass adds: The ISM policies attach via ism_template to zeek-, suricata- and arkime-/pcap-. Malcolm writes everything to arkime_sessions3-YYMMDD and malcolm_beats_, and arkime- does not match arkime_sessions3-. No policy ever attaches. Their rollover actions would also fail without a rollover_alias. daemon/storage/ilm_generator.py re-creates the same patterns at startup. The daemon's own date-based deletion runs only when disk is at or above 80% (run_cycle). _TIER_PREFIXES classifies arkime_sessions3- as 'cold' with 30 days, but that index holds all Zeek metadata and Suricata alerts.
  • Failure scenario: deploy-malcolm.sh and POST /api/ilm/apply report the policies as applied, but OpenSearch never ages anything out. Retention then depends only on the daemon pruner, which treats arkime_sessions3 (all Zeek metadata and Suricata alerts) as 30-day cold data, not the advertised 90-day/180-day tiers, and never prunes malcolm_beats_* by age.
  • Fix: Point the policy at arkime_sessions3-* (and malcolm_beats_*) and remove the rollover actions (indices are daily), or stop shipping and applying the static policy and let the daemon's ILM worker own retention. Fix the daemon tier mapping for arkime_sessions3. (effort M)

docs.title: LD-001 (HIGH) — Boot units written by the daemon are never enabled: the wants/ symlinks point at the container path
docs.text:
• Where: daemon/services/bridge_manager.py:635, daemon/services/mirror_manager.py:550
  • Verdict: CONFIRMED. Read directly by the lead while designing the DHCP mode; not run on hardware.
  • Tracked: new
  • Issue: BridgeManager and MirrorManager write nettap-bridge.service / nettap-mirror.service into the host mount /host/etc/systemd/system and then create multi-user.target.wants/ with os.symlink(unit_path, ...), where unit_path is the container path /host/etc/systemd/system/. On the host that symlink target does not exist, so systemd treats the unit as missing and never starts it at boot.
  • Failure scenario: Bridge created from Go Live, host reboots: the oneshot that forces br0 UP, sets promisc and disables bridge netfilter never runs. If the networkd race (LP#1874022) leaves br0 down, the household has no internet after a reboot. Mirror mode: the capture NIC is not flushed / promisc at boot.
  • Fix: Create the symlink with the host path as target (/etc/systemd/system/) or a relative target (../); use os.path.lexists when replacing. The DHCP gateway unit on phase-4/dhcp-gateway-mode already does this. (effort S)

docs.title: MS-003 (HIGH) — A disabled packet-capture setting is turned back on at every boot
docs.text:
• Where: docker/docker-compose.yml:473
  • Verdict: CONFIRMED. main.py calls enforce_capture_state once, right after start_api returns. It runs docker stop nettap-pcap-capture when PCAP_CAPTURE_ENABLED=false. pcap-capture depends on nettap-storage-daemon being service_healthy, and that cannot happen before the API is up and a healthcheck probe passes. During docker compose up -d (run on every boot after the unit's ExecStop down), the pcap-capture container is only Created, so docker stop is a no-op. Compose then starts it once the daemon is healthy, and nothing re-enforces the setting.
  • Tracked: new
  • Related: CR-020
  • Issue: The daemon enforces PCAP_CAPTURE_ENABLED=false at startup with docker stop nettap-pcap-capture (enforce_capture_state in main.py, called right after the API starts). But pcap-capture has depends_on nettap-storage-daemon: service_healthy, and the daemon's first healthcheck runs about 30s after start. On docker compose up -d, which nettap.service runs on every boot after its ExecStop down, the stop hits a created-but-not-started container. Compose then starts pcap-capture once the daemon turns healthy.
  • Failure scenario: The user turns raw PCAP capture off in the UI, for privacy or disk reasons. After the next reboot, netsniff-ng is capturing full payloads on br0 again while the UI still reads 'disabled', and disk use climbs.
  • Fix: Enforce capture state after compose has started the container: retry the stop until it succeeds, or poll the container state in the daemon's loop. Better, make the persisted setting authoritative at compose level, e.g. PCAP_ENABLE_NETSNIFF=${PCAP_CAPTURE_ENABLED:-true} from the env file, or a compose profile. (effort S)

docs.title: MS-004 (HIGH) — arkime-live has no curlrc mount, so it hangs forever and never captures or initialises the DB
docs.text:
• Where: docker/docker-compose.yml:518
  • Verdict: CONFIRMED. arkime-live's only volume is pcap-data:/data/pcap. Upstream bind-mounts .opensearch.primary.curlrc into arkime-live. Without it, opensearch_status.sh builds no CURL_CONFIG_PARAMS, so its first loop (curl --head --fail $OPENSEARCH_URL, without --insecure and without credentials) can never succeed against the self-signed, authenticated localhost:9200. live_capture.sh prints 'Giving $OPENSEARCH_PRIMARY time to start...' and then blocks on opensearch_status.sh -t malcolm_template. initarkime.sh also autostarts (ARKIME_PCAP_PROCESSOR defaults to true and is not overridden) and blocks on opensearch_status.sh before db.pl init. As a result arkime_sessions3_template is never created, and dashboards-helper's shared-object-creation stays blocked on it.
  • Tracked: partially: commit dbd2c64 claimed to fix 'arkime can't reach OpenSearch'; the f…
  • Issue: arkime-live gets OPENSEARCH_CREDS_CONFIG_FILE=/var/local/curlrc/.opensearch.primary.curlrc from the *opensearch-env anchor, but its only volume is pcap-data. Upstream mounts the curlrc into arkime-live. Without it, docker_entrypoint.sh builds elasticsearch=https://:@localhost:9200. live_capture.sh and initarkime.sh call opensearch_status.sh, which gets no insecure flag and no credentials from the missing curlrc. Its first loop (curl --head --fail https://localhost:9200) fails TLS verification against Malcolm's self-signed CA forever. The container has no healthcheck, so it shows as 'Up'. The partial fix in commit dbd2c64 changed only the URL.
  • Failure scenario: docker logs nettap-arkime-live stops at 'Giving opensearch-local time to start...'. db.pl init never runs, so there are no arkime_* indices and no arkime_sessions3_template. Capture never starts and no Arkime sessions are indexed. dashboards-helper's shared-object-creation.sh blocks forever on opensearch_status.sh -l arkime_sessions3_template, so the correct malcolm_template, index patterns and Malcolm dashboards are never created.
  • Fix: Add - ./curlrc:/var/local/curlrc:ro to arkime-live. Add Malcolm's healthcheck (/usr/local/bin/container_health.sh) to arkime-live, zeek-live, suricata-live and pcap-capture so silent hangs show up. Decide whether Arkime or netsniff owns full capture (see the PCAP finding) before enabling both. (effort S)

docs.title: MS-005 (HIGH) — malcolm_template is pushed with a literal REPLACER index pattern, so it never applies
docs.text:
• Where: scripts/install/deploy-malcolm.sh:521
  • Verdict: CONFIRMED. bootstrap_index_templates PUTs /opt/templates/malcolm_template.json as-is. That file (dashboards/templates/malcolm_template.json) has index_patterns ["MALCOLM_NETWORK_INDEX_PATTERN_REPLACER"]. Only shared-object-creation.sh's DoReplacersInFile substitutes the pattern, shards/replicas/refresh and _meta.hash. That script first blocks on opensearch_status.sh -l arkime_sessions3_template, which only Arkime's db.pl init creates, and that never runs (see claim 4). Nothing else in NetTap pushes a corrected template. Repo history backs this up: the daemon needs .keyword suffixes everywhere, and the event.id long-vs-string mapper_parsing_exception was 'fixed' by editing malcolm_template, which cannot take effect because the template matches no index.
  • Tracked: DEPLOYMENT-ISSUES Chain 13 and Chain 16.14 (symptoms only; root cause is new)
  • Issue: bootstrap_index_templates PUTs /opt/templates/malcolm_template.json raw. That file's index_patterns is ["MALCOLM_NETWORK_INDEX_PATTERN_REPLACER"]. Malcolm's shared-object-creation.sh runs DoReplacersInFile (substituting arkime_sessions3-, shard/replica/refresh settings) and stores a _meta.hash before pushing. The template exists by name, which unblocks Logstash's opensearch_status.sh -t malcolm_template, but it matches no index. Dashboards-helper never repairs it, because its shared-object-creation first blocks on Arkime's legacy arkime_sessions3_template, which is never created (see the arkime-live finding). So arkime_sessions3- is built entirely by dynamic mapping. Malcolm's real template maps zeek.dns.query and similar fields as keyword and IPs as ip.
  • Failure scenario: Each daily index arkime_sessions3-YYMMDD gets its types from whichever document arrives first. A Suricata event with numeric event.id maps it as long, and then every Zeek doc (string UID) is rejected with mapper_parsing_exception for that whole day. This is Chain 16.14 recurring daily. Every string field becomes text+keyword, which is why the daemon needs .keyword (Chain 13). The default total_fields.limit of 1000 (the template sets 7500) can start rejecting docs carrying new fields. Malcolm Dashboards never gets its index pattern or dashboards.
  • Fix: Push the template after substituting the replacers (sed MALCOLM_NETWORK_INDEX_PATTERN_REPLACER→arkime_sessions3-, MALCOLM_OTHER_INDEX_PATTERN_REPLACER→malcolm_beats_), or run dashboards-helper's shared-object-creation.sh once (after fixing arkime). Also push malcolm_beats_template. Then roll the index or reindex, and plan the daemon migration away from .keyword suffixes: with the real template those subfields do not exist. (effort M)

docs.title: Coverage and known gaps
docs.text:
The completeness critic listed these as not reviewed deeply enough; treat them as unreviewed, not clean:

  • Arkime viewer exposure (highest-risk gap): arkime-live runs with network_mode: host and ARKIME_VIEWER_PORT 8005, so the viewer listens on every host interface, including the management IP that LAN clients can reach. Both security-crosscut and scripts-infra dropped this as unverifiable because they could not inspect Malcolm's Arkime auth (userNameHeader / requiredAuthHeader / userAuthIps). If Malcolm's viewer trusts an auth header from any source IP, any LAN host gets full-content PCAP of all household traffic. Making it worse: compose falls back to ARKIME_PASSWORD_SECRET='NetTap_Arkime_Secret', generate-secrets.sh writes to an unread /opt/nettap/.env, and the ufw deny for 8005 sits in setup-firewall.sh, which install never runs.
  • Capture-pipeline config overrides were only skimmed by every area. config/zeek/nettap.zeek is bind-mounted over Malcolm's /opt/zeek/share/zeek/site/local.zeek. It @loads 'base/files/extract-all-files', which is not a real Zeek path; it ignores the ZEEK_JSON getenv that RELIABILITY-TRACKER lesson 31 says local.zeek relies on; and replacing the file drops Malcolm's own site scripts. Three outcomes are possible and none was checked: Zeek is broken, which would fit the recent move to Arkime-native fields; Zeek silently extracts every file to disk; or the mount is dead. config/suricata/nettap.yaml is mounted at /etc/suricata/nettap.yaml, but nothing appears to include it. config/logstash/supervisord.conf and the jvm options were not reviewed.
  • Field contract with real indices: every daemon area disclaimed that its queries were never checked against a live document (Arkime-native vs Zeek ECS fields, event.provider/event.dataset filters, .keyword vs ip types, the missing 'arp' dataset, nested _source). Recent commits show this drifting. Many 'returns nothing' bugs may be hiding, and none can be confirmed from the checkout alone.
  • daemon/api/traffic.py (1276 lines, the main dashboard data source and the reference pattern in CLAUDE.md): summary, top-talkers, top-destinations and protocols (lines ~110-400) were only skimmed. daemon/api/devices_v2.py (497 lines) was grep-only in every area. No deep review of query building, input bounds or error handling on these core endpoints.
  • scripts/remote/*.sh: 26 scripts run on the device with sudo docker were only grep-checked for destructive commands. Not checked: whether deploy scripts force-recreate or down/up OpenSearch without the mandatory security bootstrap (which breaks all auth), check out stale branches (already found once in full-stack-test.sh), or use sudo bash with the $HOME pitfall.
  • No area reviewed the test suites (daemon/tests, web .test.ts, tests/scripts/.bats, web/e2e) for wrong contracts. The many daemon/web shape mismatches found (bypass_active vs active, devices vs scores, history wrapper, PATCH route) suggest the mocks encode the client's assumptions rather than the daemon's real responses, so CI gives false confidence.
  • Watchdog on an inline appliance: config/watchdog/watchdog.conf sets max-load-1 = 24 on a 4-core N100, and the box runs IO-wait-heavy OpenSearch, Suricata and Arkime. D-state load spikes could trigger hardware-watchdog reboots, and every reboot cuts the household's internet. The config was only skimmed.
  • Shared .env writes: settings, setup and storage _sync_env each write .env non-atomically with different quoting. Two areas noticed this in their dropped lists, but nobody traced whether that .env is the one docker compose reads on nettap.service start. If it is, a torn or misquoted write could keep the whole stack down after a reboot.
  • Web client and utility code reviewed shallowly or not at all: web/src/lib/api/{mac-correlation,lan-security,logs,geoip,lookup,notification-hub,reports}.ts in depth, and web/src/lib/utils/{tshark-filter,tshark-analyze,tshark-helpers,thresholds}.ts. Shared components SessionTimeline, SankeyDiagram, PacketTable and the tshark panes were only skimmed.

The gap pass the critic requested ran on: docker/docker-compose.yml (services arkime-live, zeek-live, suricata-live, pcap-capture, logstash, filebeat, nginx-proxy: env, network_mode, volumes, entrypoints); config/zeek/nettap.zeek; config/suricata/nettap.yaml; config/suricata/update-sources.yaml; config/logstash/supervisord.conf; config/logstash/jvm.options.d/99-nettap.options; scripts/install/malcolm-config.sh (ARKIME_SECRET, NGINX_AUTH_MODE, generated compose .env); scripts/install/setup-firewall.sh (port 8005/8880 rules) and scripts/install/install.sh (whether the firewall step runs); Debugging/RELIABILITY-TRACKER.md lessons 29-35 for context. Cross-check every claim against upstream Malcolm at the pinned tag 26.02.0 (e.g. gh api repos/idaholab/Malcolm/contents/<path>?ref=v26.02.0, or the matching tag name): arkime/etc/config.ini and the arkime entrypoint/supervisord scripts, zeek/config/local.zeek and the zeek supervisord/entrypoint, and suricata config generation (suricata_config_populate.py or equivalent).. The Malcolm-stack pass then covered the capture/OpenSearch/Logstash/Filebeat/Arkime/Grafana configuration in depth.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text: NetTap uses Suricata as its intrusion detection system (IDS), monitoring all network traffic for known malicious patterns using the Emerging Threats Open ruleset.

docs.title: Understanding Alerts
docs.text:
An alert fires when network traffic matches a Suricata detection rule. Each alert includes:

  • Signature --- the rule name describing what was detected (e.g., "ET MALWARE Known Malicious User-Agent")
  • Severity --- how serious the detection is
  • Source IP --- the device that initiated the connection
  • Destination IP --- the remote host
  • Protocol --- the network protocol (TCP, UDP, etc.)
  • Timestamp --- when the detection occurred

Alerts are detections, not blocks

NetTap v1.0 is read-only. It detects and reports suspicious traffic but does not block it. Think of it as a security camera, not a security guard.

docs.title: Severity Levels
docs.text:
Suricata assigns a numeric severity (1--3) to each rule. NetTap maps these to human-readable labels:

Severity Label Badge Color Meaning 1 HIGH Red Likely malicious activity. Investigate promptly. 2 MEDIUM Yellow Potentially suspicious. May be legitimate but worth reviewing. 3 LOW Blue Informational or policy-level detection. Usually benign. (none) INFO Grey Miscellaneous detection with no severity assigned.

docs.title: What counts as an alert
docs.text:
Emerging Threats rates each of its rules as Critical, Major, Minor, Informational or Unknown. NetTap counts an alert only when ET rates it Critical, Major or Minor. Rules from other sources, and your own rules, always count.

Rules that ET rates Informational or Unknown match ordinary traffic: video-call STUN, DNS over HTTPS, apps checking for updates. NetTap still stores these. It lists them as activity, but leaves them out of every alert total, the Home page, device risk scores and the threat summary. On a home network they are usually most of what Suricata reports.

To see them, open Alerts. Under the severity tiles, the line "… informational events not counted · Show" opens the list filtered to activity. The Activity chip above the list shows the filter is on; clear it to go back to counted alerts.

docs.title: Alerts Page
docs.text: The dedicated alerts page (/alerts) provides a full-featured alert management interface.

docs.title: Severity Filter Tabs
docs.text:
Filter the alert list by severity using the tabs at the top:

  • All --- show all alerts
  • High --- show only severity 1 (red)
  • Medium --- show only severity 2 (yellow)
  • Low --- show only severity 3 (blue)

docs.title: Alert Table
docs.text: The main table displays alerts with columns for severity, signature, source IP, destination IP, protocol, and timestamp. Click any column header to sort.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text: Alerts are paginated at 50 per page. Navigation controls at the bottom let you move between pages. The total alert count is shown above the table.

docs.title: Alert Detail Panel
docs.text:
Click any alert row to open a slide-out detail panel on the right side of the screen. The detail panel shows:

  • Full signature name and description
  • Source IP and port
  • Destination IP and port
  • Protocol
  • Exact timestamp
  • Alert category
  • Raw alert data (JSON)

docs.title: Auto-Refresh
docs.text: Enable auto-refresh (30-second interval) using the toggle in the page header to see new alerts as they arrive.

docs.title: True Positives (Real Threats)
docs.text:
• Malware communication --- a device contacting known command-and-control servers
  • Exploit attempts --- traffic matching known vulnerability exploit patterns
  • Data exfiltration --- unusual outbound data transfers to suspicious destinations

docs.title: Common False Positives
docs.text:
Some alerts are triggered by legitimate traffic. Common examples:

  • "ET INFO" rules --- informational detections about normal protocols (e.g., TLS version detection)
  • "ET POLICY" rules --- policy-level detections (e.g., P2P traffic, VPN usage)
  • Gaming and streaming --- some game and streaming protocols trigger low-severity rules
  • IoT devices --- smart home devices sometimes use non-standard protocols that trigger alerts

Evaluating alerts

When investigating an alert:

  1. Check the severity --- HIGH alerts deserve immediate attention
  2. Read the signature --- the rule name usually explains what was detected
  3. Look at the source IP --- is it one of your devices or external?
  4. Check the destination --- is it a known legitimate service?
  5. Look for patterns --- a single alert is less concerning than repeated alerts from the same device

docs.title: Alert Volume
docs.text:
On a typical home network, you should expect:

  • 0--5 HIGH alerts per day (investigate all of these)
  • 5--20 MEDIUM alerts per day (review periodically)
  • 20--100+ LOW/INFO alerts per day (normal background noise)
  • Thousands of activity events per day (ET Informational; listed, not counted)

If you see significantly more HIGH alerts than expected, it could indicate a compromised device on your network.

docs.title: Where Alerts Come From
docs.text:
The alert pipeline:

  1. Raw packets traverse the br0 bridge
  2. Suricata captures and inspects packets in real-time using the rule sources listed below
  3. Matching packets generate alert events in eve.json
  4. Filebeat ships eve.json logs to Logstash
  5. Logstash enriches and forwards to OpenSearch
  6. NetTap dashboard queries OpenSearch and displays alerts

docs.title: Rule sources
docs.text:
Suricata uses four free rule sources:

Source What it catches Emerging Threats Open (et/open) The general ruleset: malware, exploits, scans, policy abuse.ch SSL Blacklist (abuse.ch/sslbl-blacklist) TLS certificates used by malware command servers Echap stalkerware indicators (echap/stalkerware) Domains that stalkerware apps report to IPFire DBL (ipfire/dbl) Malware and phishing domains only

IPFire's other categories (ads, gambling, DNS over HTTPS and so on) are turned off on purpose: they flag ordinary browsing. Settings › Suricata rules lists the sources Suricata really runs.

docs.title: When rules update
docs.text: Rules update when Suricata starts, every night at 00:00 UTC, and when you press Update now on Settings › Suricata rules. An update is kept only if Suricata loads it with no failed rules. If a download fails or a rule doesn't load, Suricata keeps the last good rules, and the page says why the update failed. After 48 hours without a successful update the status turns amber.

docs.title: Emerging Threats Pro (optional)
docs.text:
If you have a paid Emerging Threats Pro code from Proofpoint, enter it on Settings › Suricata rules. NetTap checks the code with Proofpoint first and saves it only if Proofpoint accepts it. Suricata then restarts and downloads ET Pro instead of ET Open; this takes a few minutes and the page follows it. The code stays on the appliance (/etc/nettap/suricata.env, readable by root only) and is never shown again or written to a log. Remove code goes back to ET Open.

When the code expires, every nightly update fails until you renew or remove it; Suricata keeps the last good rules meanwhile.

docs.title: Your own rules
docs.text:
Settings › Suricata rules has a box for your own Suricata rules, one per line (lines starting with # are notes). They raise alerts like any other rule and always count. What you can use:

  • Only alert rules. pass, drop and reject are refused: NetTap watches traffic, it doesn't block it.
  • Each rule needs its own sid from 1000000 to 1999999. No rule source uses that range.
  • No keywords that run code, change the engine or touch files: lua, luajit, luaxform, config, bypass, dataset, datarep, datajson, filestore, filemd5, filesha1, filesha256 and tls.store.
  • Up to 2,000 rules and 256 KB of text, and up to 8,190 bytes on one line.
  • Write each rule the way Suricata reads it. Start each rule at the start of its line. Don't end a line with \, because Suricata joins it to the next line. Use only tabs, spaces and line breaks; no other control characters. Put \ before a ; that is part of a value, even inside quotes (content:"a\;b";): Suricata ends an option at every ; that has no \ before it. Lists in [ ] can't contain spaces.

Check rules runs NetTap's checks without saving. Save and load checks again, then has Suricata test your rules together with every installed rule in a separate, throwaway copy; only if that test passes are they put in place and loaded. A refused rule is shown on its line with Suricata's reason, and nothing changes. If Suricata can't load saved rules, the previous ones are put back. A save can take a few minutes; it waits for a rule update that is running, and Update now waits for a save.

To remove all your rules, clear the box and save. The previous version is kept as owner.rules.prev on the suricata-custom-rules volume.

Example: alert when any device looks up example.invalid:

alert dns any any -> any any (msg:"Lookup of example.invalid"; dns.query; content:"example.invalid"; nocase; sid:1000001; rev:1;)

docs.title: Dashboard Overview
docs.text: The NetTap dashboard provides a real-time view of your network activity. This page explains each panel and how to use them.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: The dashboard is organized into rows of information, following a progressive disclosure pattern: big numbers first, details on drill-down.

docs.title: Header Bar
docs.text:
The top of the dashboard shows:

  • Network Overview title and subtitle
  • Last updated timestamp showing when data was last fetched
  • Auto-refresh toggle --- enabled by default at 30-second intervals. Click to pause/resume.
  • Refresh button --- manually trigger a data refresh

docs.title: Filter Bar
docs.text:
Below the header, the filter bar lets you narrow the dashboard to specific time ranges, devices, or protocols:

  • Time range --- presets (1h, 6h, 24h, 7d, 30d) or custom date range
  • Device filter --- filter by a specific IP address
  • Protocol filter --- filter by protocol (TCP, UDP, DNS, HTTP, TLS, etc.)

docs.title: Row 1: Stat Cards
docs.text: Five summary cards across the top provide at-a-glance metrics:

docs.title: Total Bandwidth (24h)
docs.text:
Shows the total bytes transferred across your network in the selected time period. Breaks down into inbound and outbound traffic below the main number.

A trend indicator (up/down arrow with percentage) compares to the previous equivalent time period. For example, if you're viewing 24 hours, the trend compares to the 24 hours before that.

docs.title: Connections (24h)
docs.text: Total number of network connections observed. Shows the most common protocol below the count (e.g., "Top protocol: TLS").

docs.title: Alerts (24h)
docs.text: Number of Suricata IDS detections in the selected period. The subtitle breaks down by severity: high, medium, and low. Click "View all" to go to the full Alerts page.

docs.title: System Health
docs.text:
Shows the overall health status of the NetTap system:

  • Healthy (green) --- all systems operational
  • Degraded (yellow) --- one or more subsystems have issues

Below the badge, it shows OpenSearch connectivity status.

docs.title: Devices
docs.text: Count of unique devices (IP addresses) observed on your network. This tells you how many devices are actively generating traffic.

docs.title: Bandwidth Over Time
docs.text:
A time-series line chart showing bytes transferred per hour over the selected time range. Hover over any point to see the exact timestamp and value.

This chart is useful for identifying:

  • Usage patterns --- when your network is busiest
  • Anomalies --- unexpected spikes in traffic
  • Trends --- whether bandwidth usage is increasing over time

docs.title: Protocol Distribution
docs.text:
A donut chart showing the breakdown of connections by protocol. The top 6 protocols are shown with distinct colors:

  • Blue: primary protocol (usually TLS or DNS)
  • Green, amber, red, purple, light blue: subsequent protocols
  • Grey: "other" (aggregated remaining protocols)

docs.title: Row 2.5: Traffic Categories
docs.text:
A horizontal bar chart categorizing traffic by type:

  • Streaming (Netflix, YouTube, Twitch)
  • Social Media (Facebook, Instagram, TikTok)
  • Gaming (Steam, Xbox Live, PlayStation Network)
  • Productivity (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365)
  • Cloud (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud)
  • Messaging (WhatsApp, Slack, Discord)
  • News, Shopping, Email, and more

Each bar shows the relative bandwidth consumed by that category. This section only appears when traffic category data is available.

docs.title: Top Talkers
docs.text:
A ranked table of the most active source IP addresses by bandwidth:

Column Description # Rank (1--10) Source IP The device's IP address (with hostname tooltip if available) Bandwidth Total bytes transferred Connections Number of connections from this device

IP addresses are displayed as interactive elements --- hover for additional details, click to navigate to the device's detail page.

docs.title: Recent Alerts
docs.text:
The 10 most recent Suricata IDS detections:

Column Description Severity Color-coded badge: HIGH (red), MEDIUM (yellow), LOW (blue), INFO (grey) Signature The Suricata rule that triggered the alert Source Source IP address Dest Destination IP address

Click any alert row to open the Alert Detail Panel --- a slide-out panel on the right showing full alert details including:

  • Complete alert signature and description
  • Source and destination IPs with port numbers
  • Protocol details
  • Timestamp
  • The raw alert data

docs.title: Other Dashboard Pages
docs.text:
The navigation sidebar provides access to additional pages:

Page Path Description Alerts /alerts Full alert management with filtering, pagination, and detail view Devices /devices Sortable, searchable device inventory Device Detail /devices/{ip} Deep-dive into a specific device's activity Connections /connections Connection log explorer Investigations /investigations Bookmark and annotate suspicious activity Compliance /compliance Security compliance posture overview Settings /settings System configuration Notifications /settings/notifications Email, webhook, and in-app alert configuration System /system Hardware health, storage, service status Updates /system/updates Software version inventory and update management Setup /setup Re-run the setup wizard CyberChef /system/cyberchef Data transformation and decoding tool

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Loading skeletons --- when data is loading, you will see animated placeholder shapes. This is normal during initial load or after changing filters.
  • Error banner --- if the dashboard cannot reach the monitoring daemon, an orange warning banner appears at the top. Check that the nettap-storage-daemon container is running.
  • Empty states --- "No traffic data available" or "No alerts detected. All clear." messages appear when there is no data for the selected time range. Give the system time to collect data after initial setup.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: NetTap can send notifications when significant events occur, such as high-severity IDS alerts or system health issues. Three notification channels are supported.

docs.title: Email (SMTP)
docs.text:
Send alert notifications to one or more email addresses via SMTP.

Configuration (via dashboard at /settings/notifications):

Setting Description Default SMTP Host Your SMTP server address (empty --- disabled) SMTP Port SMTP port 587 SMTP User SMTP authentication username (empty) SMTP Password SMTP authentication password (empty) From Address Sender email address nettap@localhost Recipients Comma-separated list of email addresses (empty)

Via environment variables:

.env
SMTP_HOST=smtp.gmail.com
SMTP_PORT=587
SMTP_USER=your-email@gmail.com
SMTP_PASS=your-app-password
ALERT_EMAIL=admin@example.com

Gmail App Passwords

If using Gmail, you need to generate an App Password rather than using your regular Gmail password. Enable 2-factor authentication first, then create an App Password for "Mail."

docs.title: Webhook
docs.text:
Send JSON payloads to a URL when alerts fire. This works with:

  • Slack (via incoming webhook URLs)
  • Discord (via webhook URLs)
  • Microsoft Teams (via incoming webhook connectors)
  • PagerDuty, Opsgenie, or any HTTP endpoint

Configuration:

Setting Description Webhook URL The endpoint to POST alert data to

Via environment variables:

.env
WEBHOOK_URL=https://your-webhook-service.example.com/alerts

docs.title: In-App Notifications
docs.text: In-app notifications appear in the dashboard notification bell. These are enabled by default and cannot be disabled. They provide a history of recent events within the dashboard UI.

docs.title: Severity Threshold
docs.text:
Control which alerts trigger notifications. The severity threshold determines the minimum severity level that generates notifications:

Threshold Notifies on 1 (High only) Only HIGH severity alerts 2 (Medium+) HIGH and MEDIUM alerts 3 (All) HIGH, MEDIUM, and LOW alerts

The default is 3 (all severities). For most home networks, setting this to 2 (Medium and above) reduces notification noise while still catching important events.

docs.title: Via the Dashboard
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Settings > Notifications (/settings/notifications)
  2. Enable your preferred channels (Email, Webhook, or both)
  3. Fill in the configuration fields
  4. Click Test to send a test notification
  5. Click Save to apply

docs.title: Via the API
docs.text:
# Get current notification config
curl http://localhost:8880/api/notifications/config

# Update notification config
curl -X POST http://localhost:8880/api/notifications/config \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "email": {
      "enabled": true,
      "recipients": ["admin@example.com"],
      "smtpHost": "smtp.gmail.com",
      "smtpPort": 587,
      "smtpUser": "your-email@gmail.com",
      "smtpPass": "your-app-password",
      "smtpFrom": "nettap@yourdomain.com"
    },
    "webhook": {
      "enabled": true,
      "url": "https://your-webhook-service.example.com/alerts"
    },
    "severityThreshold": 2
  }'

docs.title: Testing Notifications
docs.text:
From the Notifications settings page, use the Test button to send a test notification through each configured channel. This verifies that:

  • SMTP credentials are correct and the mail server is reachable
  • Webhook URLs are valid and accept POST requests
  • Email recipients receive the test message

docs.title: Notification Content
docs.text:
Alert notifications include:

  • Alert severity (HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW)
  • Signature name (the Suricata rule that triggered)
  • Source and destination IPs with port numbers
  • Timestamp of the detection
  • Link to the alert in the NetTap dashboard

docs.title: SIEM Forwarding
docs.text: NetTap can forward logs to an external SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) system for centralized security monitoring. This is useful if you already run a SIEM like Splunk, Elastic SIEM, Wazuh, or QRadar and want to include NetTap's network telemetry.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
NetTap's log pipeline already includes Logstash as part of the Malcolm stack. Logstash can be configured to send copies of all logs to external destinations in addition to the local OpenSearch cluster.

Zeek / Suricata ──> Filebeat ──> Logstash ──┬──> OpenSearch (local)
                                             └──> External SIEM

docs.title: Syslog Output
docs.text:
Forward logs via syslog (TCP or UDP) to any syslog-compatible receiver:

Add a Logstash output configuration:

config/logstash/siem-output.conf
output {
  syslog {
    host => "siem.example.com"
    port => 514
    protocol => "tcp"
    facility => "local0"
    severity => "informational"
    sourcehost => "nettap"
    msgid => "%{[event][module]}"
  }
}

docs.title: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch Output
docs.text:
Forward to a remote Elasticsearch or OpenSearch cluster:

config/logstash/siem-output.conf
output {
  elasticsearch {
    hosts => ["https://siem.example.com:9200"]
    index => "nettap-%{[event][module]}-%{+YYYY.MM.dd}"
    user => "logstash_writer"
    password => "your-password"
    ssl => true
    cacert => "/path/to/ca.crt"
  }
}

docs.title: HTTP Output
docs.text:
Forward to any HTTP endpoint (useful for cloud SIEMs):

config/logstash/siem-output.conf
output {
  http {
    url => "https://siem.example.com/api/v1/logs"
    http_method => "post"
    format => "json"
    headers => {
      "Authorization" => "Bearer your-api-token"
      "Content-Type" => "application/json"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Kafka Output
docs.text:
For high-volume environments, forward via Kafka:

config/logstash/siem-output.conf
output {
  kafka {
    bootstrap_servers => "kafka.example.com:9092"
    topic_id => "nettap-logs"
    codec => json
  }
}

docs.title: 1. Create the Output Configuration
docs.text:
Create a Logstash pipeline configuration file for your SIEM:

mkdir -p /opt/nettap/config/logstash
nano /opt/nettap/config/logstash/siem-output.conf

docs.title: 2. Mount the Configuration
docs.text:
Add the configuration file as a volume mount in docker/docker-compose.yml for the Logstash service:

logstash:
  volumes:
    # ... existing volumes ...
    - ../config/logstash/siem-output.conf:/usr/share/logstash/pipeline/siem-output.conf:ro

docs.title: 3. Restart Logstash
docs.text: docker compose -f /opt/nettap/docker/docker-compose.yml restart logstash

docs.title: 4. Verify
docs.text:
Check Logstash logs to confirm the output plugin loaded successfully:

docker logs nettap-logstash --tail 50

Look for messages indicating the new output pipeline is active.

docs.title: Data Format
docs.text:
Logs forwarded to your SIEM contain structured JSON with these common fields:

Field Description Example event.module Source module zeek, suricata event.dataset Log type conn, dns, alert source.ip Source IP address 192.168.1.42 destination.ip Destination IP address 93.184.216.34 source.port Source port 54321 destination.port Destination port 443 network.protocol Protocol tcp, udp @timestamp Event timestamp 2026-02-26T10:30:00.000Z

Zeek and Suricata logs follow the Elastic Common Schema (ECS) field naming where possible, making integration with ECS-compatible SIEMs straightforward.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
To forward only specific log types (e.g., only alerts, not all conn logs), add a conditional to the output:

config/logstash/siem-output.conf
output {
  if [event][module] == "suricata" and [event][dataset] == "alert" {
    syslog {
      host => "siem.example.com"
      port => 514
      protocol => "tcp"
    }
  }
}

This forwards only Suricata alerts, significantly reducing the volume sent to your SIEM.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• Bandwidth: Forwarding all Zeek metadata generates 300--800 MB/day of additional network traffic to your SIEM.
  • Logstash memory: If the SIEM destination is slow or unreachable, Logstash will buffer events in its persistent queue. Ensure adequate disk space for the logstash-persistent-queue Docker volume.
  • Filtering recommended: For most use cases, forwarding only Suricata alerts and DNS logs provides high security value at a fraction of the data volume.

docs.title: Storage Management
docs.text: NetTap uses a three-tier storage architecture to balance retention needs with disk space. This page explains how storage works and how to manage it.

docs.title: Three-Tier Storage Architecture
docs.text: Tier Data Default Retention Where it lives Hot Zeek logs and Suricata alerts 90 days (RETENTION_HOT) One daily OpenSearch index, arkime_sessions3-YYMMDD Warm Separate suricata-* indices only 180 days (RETENTION_WARM) Not created by a Malcolm install, so this setting is normally unused Cold PCAP captures (all traffic) 30 days (RETENTION_COLD) Files under /opt/nettap/pcap, capped at PCAP_MAX_DISK_PCT of the disk

docs.title: Hot Tier (Zeek logs and Suricata alerts)
docs.text:
Malcolm's Logstash writes every Zeek log (conn, DNS, HTTP, TLS, DHCP, SMTP, files) and every Suricata alert into the same daily index.

  • Index pattern: arkime_sessions3-* (plus malcolm_beats_* host data, if present)
  • Retention: 90 days by default (RETENTION_HOT). The whole daily index is deleted, so alerts are kept exactly as long as Zeek logs.
  • Action at expiry: automatic deletion by the nettap-hot-policy ISM policy.

docs.title: Warm Tier (separate Suricata indices)
docs.text: The daemon keeps a warm retention setting for suricata-* indices, but a standard install never creates them: alerts go into the hot index above. To keep alerts longer, raise the hot retention.

docs.title: Cold Tier (PCAP Captures)
docs.text:
netsniff-ng records all traffic to rotating PCAP files. They are files, not OpenSearch indices.

  • Location: /opt/nettap/pcap (rotated by PCAP_ROTATE_MB or every PCAP_ROTATE_MIN minutes)
  • Retention: 30 days by default (RETENTION_COLD)
  • Disk cap: PCAP files are capped at PCAP_MAX_DISK_PCT percent of the disk (default 25; 0 disables the cap). The storage daemon deletes the oldest files first.
  • Action at expiry: the storage daemon deletes the file.

docs.title: Index Lifecycle Management (ILM)
docs.text: OpenSearch ISM (Index State Management) manages the hot indices. The daemon builds the policy from your retention settings (daemon/storage/ilm_generator.py) and applies it at startup and whenever retention is saved; config/opensearch/ilm-policy.json is the fallback.

docs.title: Policy Flow
docs.text:
nettap-hot-policy  (arkime_sessions3-*, malcolm_beats_*, zeek-*)
  hot ── after RETENTION_HOT days ──> delete

There is no rollover or force-merge: Malcolm already starts a new index each day.

All policy actions include retry logic (3 attempts with exponential backoff) to handle transient OpenSearch errors.

docs.title: Reapplying Policies
docs.text:
If you change retention settings, reapply ILM policies:

Via DashboardVia API

Go to System and use the storage management panel.

curl -X POST http://localhost:8880/api/ilm/apply

docs.title: Disk Monitoring
docs.text: The NetTap storage daemon monitors disk usage continuously and takes action to prevent the disk from filling up.

docs.title: Thresholds
docs.text:
Threshold Default Action Warning 80% Begins pruning oldest data from each tier Emergency 90% Aggressive pruning of all tiers

When disk usage exceeds the warning threshold:

  1. The daemon identifies the oldest indices in each tier
  2. Deletes indices beyond their retention period first
  3. If still above threshold, deletes the oldest indices regardless of retention

docs.title: Monitoring Interval
docs.text: The storage daemon runs a maintenance cycle every 5 minutes (configurable via STORAGE_CHECK_INTERVAL).

docs.title: Viewing Disk Status
docs.text:
Via DashboardVia APIVia Command Line

Go to System to see:

  • Disk usage (total, used, available)
  • Disk usage percentage with color-coded bar
  • Per-tier index counts and sizes
# Full storage status
curl http://localhost:8880/api/storage/status

# List all indices
curl http://localhost:8880/api/indices

# Check disk usage
df -h /

# Check OpenSearch index sizes
curl -sk https://localhost:9200/_cat/indices?v&s=store.size:desc

docs.title: SMART Health Monitoring
docs.text: NetTap monitors the SSD's SMART (Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology) attributes to detect drive health issues before they cause failures.

docs.title: Monitored Attributes
docs.text:
• Overall health status (PASSED / FAILED)
  • Temperature (current, with warning thresholds)
  • Percentage used (NVMe wear indicator)
  • Power-on hours
  • Unsafe shutdowns
  • Media errors

docs.title: Viewing SMART Status
docs.text:
Go to System in the dashboard, or query the API:

curl http://localhost:8880/api/smart/health

docs.title: SSD Write Protection
docs.text:
NetTap includes several measures to extend SSD lifespan:

  • 30-second log flush intervals --- Zeek batches log writes instead of writing per-event
  • Write coalescing --- logs are compressed (zstd) before being written to OpenSearch
  • Docker log rotation --- container logs are capped at 10 MB with 3 rotations maximum

docs.title: Via Environment Variables
docs.text:
Edit .env and restart:

.env
RETENTION_HOT=90              # Zeek metadata (days)
RETENTION_WARM=180            # Suricata alerts (days)
RETENTION_COLD=30             # PCAP captures (days)
DISK_THRESHOLD_PERCENT=80     # Start pruning at this disk usage

sudo systemctl restart nettap

docs.title: Storage Sizing Guide
docs.text: Network Size Daily Data 1 TB Drive Lasts Small home (5--10 devices) ~400 MB/day 3+ years Medium home (15--25 devices) ~800 MB/day 2+ years Small office (25--50 devices) ~1.5 GB/day 1+ year Heavy use / large office ~3+ GB/day Adjust retention or add storage

docs.title: Trigger a Manual Prune Cycle
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8880/api/storage/prune

This runs the same maintenance cycle that normally executes every 5 minutes, but immediately.

docs.title: Delete Specific Indices
docs.text:
If you need to free space urgently, delete specific OpenSearch indices:

# List indices sorted by size
curl -sk https://localhost:9200/_cat/indices?v&s=store.size:desc

# Delete a specific index
curl -sk -X DELETE https://localhost:9200/zeek-2024.01.15

Data loss

Deleting indices permanently removes that data. There is no undo unless you have a backup.

docs.title: Traffic Analysis
docs.text: NetTap captures and analyzes all network traffic passing through the bridge using Zeek. This page explains the traffic analysis features and how to investigate network activity.

docs.title: Zeek Metadata
docs.text:
Zeek generates structured JSON logs for every connection and protocol interaction:

Log Type What It Captures conn Every TCP/UDP connection: source, destination, ports, duration, bytes transferred dns DNS queries and responses (what domains your devices look up) http HTTP requests and responses (method, URL, status code, user agent) ssl/tls TLS handshakes (server name, certificate details, JA3 fingerprints) dhcp DHCP leases (which devices received IP addresses) smtp Email metadata (sender, recipient, subject) files File transfers detected in any protocol (hashes, MIME types, sizes)

No payload inspection

NetTap does not decrypt or inspect encrypted traffic content. For TLS connections, Zeek records the handshake metadata (server name, certificate, JA3) but not the encrypted payload.

docs.title: Device Inventory
docs.text: The Devices page (/devices) provides a sortable, searchable table of all discovered network devices.

docs.title: Device Table Columns
docs.text: Column Description IP Address The device's IP address on your network Hostname Reverse-DNS or DHCP hostname, if available Manufacturer OUI lookup from the device's MAC address Connections Total connection count Bandwidth Total bytes transferred Last Seen When the device was last active

docs.title: Searching and Sorting
docs.text:
• Search bar --- filter by IP address, hostname, or manufacturer name
  • Column sorting --- click any column header to sort ascending/descending
  • Auto-refresh --- toggle 30-second refresh to see new devices appear

docs.title: Device Detail Page
docs.text:
Click any device row to navigate to /devices/{ip} for a deep-dive into that device's activity:

  • Connection history over time
  • Top destinations contacted
  • Protocol breakdown
  • Alert history for this device
  • Risk score

docs.title: Connections Page
docs.text:
The Connections page (/connections) provides a log explorer for individual network connections. Each connection record includes:

  • Source and destination IP + port
  • Protocol
  • Duration
  • Bytes in/out
  • Connection state (established, closed, reset, etc.)
  • Timestamp

docs.title: Traffic Categories
docs.text:
NetTap classifies traffic into human-readable categories based on destination hostnames and IP reputation data:

Category Examples Streaming Netflix, YouTube, Twitch, Spotify Social Media Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Twitter/X Gaming Steam, Xbox Live, PlayStation Network, Epic Games Productivity Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Notion Cloud AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Cloudflare Messaging WhatsApp, Slack, Discord, Telegram News CNN, BBC, Reddit, Hacker News Shopping Amazon, eBay, Shopify stores Email Gmail, Outlook, ProtonMail

The dashboard home page shows a horizontal bar chart of bandwidth by category.

docs.title: Natural Language Search
docs.text:
NetTap includes a natural language search feature that lets you query your network data in plain English:

Show me all DNS queries to suspicious domains in the last 24 hours

Which device transferred the most data yesterday?

Connections from 192.168.1.42 to external IPs last week

The search parser converts your query into an OpenSearch query and returns matching results.

docs.title: Investigations
docs.text:
The Investigations page (/investigations) lets you bookmark and annotate suspicious activity for later review:

  1. While viewing an alert, device, or connection --- click "Investigate"
  2. Add notes and tags to the investigation
  3. Review all open investigations from the Investigations page
  4. Mark investigations as resolved when done

This is useful for tracking ongoing security concerns or documenting activity for later review.

docs.title: Risk Scores
docs.text:
Each device receives a risk score from 0 (safe) to 100 (high risk) based on:

  • Number and severity of IDS alerts associated with the device
  • Communication with known-bad IP addresses or domains
  • Unusual traffic patterns or volume
  • Protocol anomalies

Risk scores update periodically as new data arrives. View risk scores on the Device Inventory page or individual Device Detail pages.

docs.title: GeoIP Mapping
docs.text:
External IP addresses are enriched with geographic location data (country, city, ASN) using MaxMind GeoLite2 databases. This helps you understand:

  • Where your traffic goes --- which countries and networks your devices communicate with
  • Unusual destinations --- connections to unexpected geographic regions
  • ISP/hosting provider identification --- via ASN lookups
